papers.abstract: Camera-controlled video generation re-renders a video along a target camera trajectory, yet moving the camera around an object, the most natural way to change the viewpoint of an object-centric scene, remains difficult. Existing methods condition either on camera parameters, which are scale-ambiguous in monocular video, or on explicit geometry such as warped point clouds or depth, which breaks down under large viewpoint changes. We present AnyCam, a method that represents the camera with an anchor object in the scene: we reconstruct it in 3D and render it along the target trajectory, a camera signal that is scale-aware, view-complete and easy to specify relative to the object. A video diffusion model transfers the content and dynamics of the source video to the new viewpoint. Its H-Concat layout aligns source and target frames in time, so the model can be distilled into AnyCam-AR, a streaming few-step generator for on-the-fly camera control. Both models are trained on paired videos with pixel-aligned anchor renderings from multi-camera videos and static-scene captures. Experiments on diverse datasets and trajectories show that AnyCam performs favorably against camera-controlled video generation and 3D reconstruction methods in camera control and visual quality.
authors: Weijie Lyu, Zhixin Shu, Yuntian Ke, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of changing viewpoints around objects, where camera parameters are scale-ambiguous and explicit geometry can fail under large viewpoint changes.
Reconstructs an anchor object in 3D and renders it along a target trajectory to represent the camera relative to the scene.
Uses a video diffusion model with H-Concat temporal alignment to transfer source-video content and dynamics to the new viewpoint.
Introduces AnyCam-AR, a streaming few-step generator for on-the-fly camera control.
Experiments across diverse datasets and trajectories show favorable camera control and visual quality compared with existing camera-controlled generation and 3D reconstruction methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of AnyCam. (a) The user selects an anchor object in the source video. SAM 2 [37] tracks it to give the source camera representation (the anchor cut-out), and SAM 3D [8] reconstructs it; the reconstruction is aligned to the source cameras and rendered along the target trajectory to give the target camera representation. The noisy target latent and the source latent are concatenated along the height (H-Concat), each half receives its camera representation through channel concatenation, and the diffusion transformer denoises the target half, which the VAE decodes into the target video. (b) The numbers under the tokens are their RoPE positions (t, h), with the role ID as a third entry in the fourth layout. The grids mark which source frames each target frame attends to. Frame concatenation [1, 7, 28] places the whole source after the target, so the first target frame needs the complete source video and therefore the generation cannot stream. Channel concatenation [15] merges the two frames into one token, which loses information and lowers fidelity to the source video [1]. Frame interleaving [52] doubles the length of the temporal axis. A shared position with a role phase [49] needs an additional positional encoding to tell the two streams apart. Our H-Concat keeps the source and target as separate tokens at the same temporal index and offsets the source in height, so the base model is used without new parameters or a custom attention mask.

Figure 10. Video-to-video comparison on CO3D. Each case takes two rows with the source frame (Input), the ground-truth frame and the frame of every method at the same time. 3DGS [20] is optimized per scene on the 81 source frames. AnyCam-AR, HY-WorldPlay [41] and InSpatio-World [40] are autoregressive models. On the sides of the objects that the source video does not show, AnyCam and AnyCam-AR match the ground truth, while 3DGS and DepthDirector [7] break down and most other baselines show the object from a wrong angle or lose it. For the television (bottom), ReDirector [30] and DepthDirector show only the floor and HY-WorldPlay shows its back.

Figure 6. Visual comparison on DAVIS. AnyCam follows every trajectory and keeps the scene intact, since the anchor rendering fixes the scale of the motion relative to the anchor and covers it from every side. Methods that warp estimated geometry show holes and stretched content at new viewpoints: TrajectoryCrafter [56] tears the airplane apart during rotation (rows 1 and 2), GEN3C [39] leaves stripes (row 2), and DepthDirector [7] breaks down under zoom-in and rise (rows 3 to 6). Methods conditioned on camera parameters guess the scale of the motion: ReCamMaster [1] loses the airplane after the orbit (row 2), Wan-Fun-Cam [44] zooms far past the train into the tree (row 4), ReDirector [30] and Wan-Fun-Cam collapse into noise under large orbit and rise (rows 2 and 6).

Figure 11. Single-image comparison on CO3D. Each block shows one case with the input image (Input), the ground-truth frame and the frame generated by each method of Tab. 3 from the same target camera. The 3D reconstruction methods render only the object and often distort its shape, e.g., LGM [42] for three of the four objects and TRELLIS [48] for the handbag and the bench. Most video generation baselines move to an incorrect viewpoint. GEN3C [39], TrajectoryCrafter [56], ReDirector [30] and Wan-Fun-Cam [44] lose the banana (top right). GEN3C, TrajectoryCrafter, DepthDirector [7], ReCamMaster [1] and ReDirector shift the sandwich (bottom right) to the right. AnyCam and AnyCam-AR match the viewpoint and the appearance of the ground truth.
Figure 21. Anchor selection prompt. System prompt given to Qwen3-VL-32B together with 8 frames of the video.

Figure 8. Long-video comparison on CO3D (left) and RealEstate10K (right). The anchor rendering gives every chunk a reference to the object, so AnyCam-AR stays registered to the scene over hundreds of frames. The baselines drift as their errors accumulate over the chunks: both lose the cellphone (left, rows 5, 6), and both turn away from the house (right, rows 1, 2) and the deck (right, rows 5, 6).

Figure 7. Single-image to video comparison on Mip-NeRF 360. Since the anchor rendering is object-relative and view-complete, AnyCam always reaches the target viewpoints. Wan-Fun-Cam [44] and ReCamMaster [1] are conditioned on camera parameters, whose scale a single photo cannot determine, and barely move away from the input view (rows 1 to 3). GEN3C [39], TrajectoryCrafter [56] and DepthDirector [7] warp a depth map that covers only the visible surface, which leaves distorted or missing content (rows 1 to 3).

Figure 4. Anchor rendering as a camera signal only. The anchor (center console) is poorly reconstructed with no texture (column 3), compared with its cut-out in the source video (column 2). AnyCam still recovers the appearance of the console and the cabin from the source video and controls the camera movement correctly, showing that the rendering only provides a camera signal and the model is robust to poor reconstructions.

Figure 12. Additional visual comparison on DAVIS (same layout as Fig. 6). The camera zooms out from the swing (rows 1 and 2) and rises by 60◦ over the display shelf, the skate bowl and the railway crossing (rows 3 to 8). AnyCam shows the whole swing frame after the zoom-out and looks down on the other three scenes. DepthDirector [7] breaks apart on the swing (rows 1 and 2) and the crossing (rows 7 and 8) and turns toward the sky above the skate bowl (rows 5 and 6). Wan-Fun-Cam [44] moves closer to the swing instead of away from it (rows 1 and 2), stays at the height of the input at the shelf (rows 3 and 4) and turns into noise on the skate bowl and the crossing (rows 6 and 8).

Figure 13. Comparison with the Plücker-ray models. Wan-Fun-Cam† and Wan-Fun-Cam-AR† are trained on our data with our recipe and receive the camera as Plücker rays instead of the anchor rendering. Top: DAVIS [32, 34] with a 60◦ rise, AnyCam and Wan-Fun-Cam†; the numbers on the input frames give the frame index. Middle: a 333-frame CO3D [38] video (166 frames out and back) generated from an 81-frame source video; bottom: a 165-frame RealEstate10K [63] video generated from a single image; AnyCam-AR and Wan-Fun-CamAR†; the labels on the ground-truth frames give the frame index and the video length. Wan-Fun-Cam† distorts the street in the last frames of the rise. Wan-Fun-Cam-AR† drifts off the bench, which the frame border cuts off from frame 94 on. On RealEstate10K, it moves into the armchair instead of toward the coffee table. AnyCam and AnyCam-AR follow the target views.

Figure 15. Failure case: small anchors. When the anchor covers only about 1% of the frame, its rendering gives little information about the rotation of the camera. For the agave plant (row 1, 0.7% of the frame), the output camera barely moves, and for the garden stool (row 2, 1.2%) it turns much less than the target orbit. Both rows show AnyCam.

Figure 2. Camera representations. Yellow represents the input camera. (a) Camera parameters are scale-ambiguous: a small object near the input camera and a large object farther away give the same input image, but the same target camera parameters (blue and red camera) see them at a different size, position and angle (blue and red boxes), so the target view is not determined. (b) A point cloud or depth warp of the input image only covers the surface seen from the input camera. Under a large viewpoint change, views are often heavily distorted (red box). The points in the target view sometimes come from the inside of the object or from the back of the image (blue box). The renderings are wrong and mislead the subsequent video generation. (c) Our anchor rendering uses the complete reconstructed object, so target cameras at any angle (green) see the whole anchor with the correct size and pose.
Figure 5. Training samples. Top: MultiCamVideo [1], a dynamic scene captured by two synchronized cameras. Bottom: DL3DV [24], two clips of a static capture.

Figure 9. CO3D target trajectories of the three difficulty levels for one sequence (hydrant), seen from above. Positions are normalized by the median radius of the source cameras. The target camera moves from source frame 0 to the first real target camera (dotted) and then follows real CO3D cameras, with ground truth at the dots.

Figure 14. Moving and deforming anchors. The anchor need not be static or rigid: a swimming swan (DAVIS [32, 34], row 1), a walking dinosaur (row 2), and a person from the DyCheck dataset [9] (bottom left: holding a teddy bear; bottom right: sitting in a chair). The condition renders the anchor reconstructed from one frame, while the generated video keeps the motion of the source, e.g., the swimming swan, the walking legs, and the moving hands and arms. Row 2 shows AnyCam-AR; all other examples show AnyCam.

Figure 16. Different anchors in the same video. For each source video, the user picks two or three objects as anchors and a target trajectory around each of them. The tags above each example name the anchors and their trajectories. Each anchor has its own trajectory, so the rows show camera control through different objects of one video, not one camera applied to several anchors. Each condition renders only its anchor. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index. All outputs are from AnyCam. In the first video, the camera pushes in toward the mirrorless camera or the instant camera on the table, or pulls back and rises over the armchair. In the second video, it orbits around the food truck toward its front or pushes in to the sandwich board.

Figure 17. Different anchors in the same video (continued). Same setting as Fig. 16. All outputs are from AnyCam. In the gaming room, the output orbits around the gaming chair or moves toward the PC tower. In the second video, it orbits around the carved armchair or rises over the side table.

Figure 18. Different anchors in the same video (continued). Same setting as Fig. 16. All outputs are from AnyCam. The output moves toward the telephone or the perfume bottle while the person keeps moving as in the source. In the studio, it rises over the writing desk or turns toward the stool.

Figure 19. The anchor leaves the frame. The camera moves past anchor A until A leaves the view; starting at the switch frame, the condition renders anchor B, a second object reconstructed from the first source frame, and the camera continues toward it. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index; tags A and B mark the anchor in the condition. All rows show AnyCam. The output keeps moving after A has left and approaches anchor B (the sports car, the red car, the white SUV and the PC tower in rows 1 to 4).

Figure 20. Switching the anchor during a video. The target camera follows one continuous trajectory. The condition renders anchor A up to frame 32 and anchor B from frame 33 (tags A and B), and both anchors are reconstructed from the first source frame. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index. Rows 1 to 3 show AnyCam, row 4 shows AnyCam-AR. After the switch, the output moves toward the side table, the perfume bottle, the bentwood chair and the PC tower.

Table 4. Single-image comparison on Mip-NeRF 360. AnyCam is best on all ground-truth metrics and FID.

Long videos on CO3D, all metrics. 30 sequences; the source is an 81-frame clip played forward and backward to the target length, and the target follows the real CO3D cameras around the object for 165 or 249 frames, or for 166 frames and back (333 frames). Best in bold, second underlined, ranked within each group.

Table 7. Attention fine-tuning versus LoRA. LoRA [16] of rank 32 on the attention and feed-forward layers, trained with a learning rate of 10−4, versus fine-tuning the self-attention layers and the patch embedding with a learning rate of 5 × 10−5. Both are trained on the same data for 10K steps with a batch size of 32. The attention fine-tuning row is AnyCam; the cases and metrics are those of its DAVIS and CO3D comparisons (Tabs. 1 and 2). papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for camera-controlled video generation using 3D reconstruction of an anchor object, fitting Video Diffusion and 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: AnyCam: Anything Can Represent Camera for Video Generation
papers.tldr: AnyCam enables camera-controlled video generation by using a reconstructed 3D anchor object to specify scale-aware, view-complete camera motion.

papers.abstract: Image editing models can follow a wide range of instructions, but video editing models still lag behind, limited in part by the difficulty of collecting paired source and edited videos. Is it possible to transfer advanced image editing capabilities to video editors without new paired videos? We introduce Image-to-Video Transfer (I2VT), which improves pretrained video editors and expands them to new editing tasks using an image editor. It enables efficient post-training with no architectural changes and no new videos, using only individual images. Our key idea is to let the video editor role-play as an image editor: it edits an image as a one-frame video, with the image editor guiding the video editor's predictions at each denoising step. Although the video editor sees only single images during training, at test time it applies the improved and expanded capabilities to whole video clips while preserving temporal consistency. To push the boundaries of video editing, we introduce OpenVE++, an extension of OpenVE-Bench that adds four new editing tasks useful for video production, including action changes, expression changes, body movements, and scene relighting. Our experiments across three different video editors show that I2VT improves existing editing capabilities and expands them to new tasks, and our models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on both OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++.
authors: Ji Xie, Yanhao Jia, Xiangpeng Yang, Martin Q. Ma, Sihan Xu, Erik Cambria, Louis-Philippe Morency
bullets: Addresses the lack of paired source–edited videos for training video editors.
Uses an image editor to guide a video editor’s frame-level predictions during denoising, with no architectural changes or new videos.
Applies the resulting capabilities to full video clips at test time while maintaining temporal consistency.
Introduces OpenVE++, extending OpenVE-Bench with action, expression, body-movement, and scene-relighting edits.
Experiments across three video editors report improved existing capabilities, broader task coverage, and SOTA performance on OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++.

Figure 2. Motivation and intuition. Left: image editors handle complex edits such as actions and relighting on single frames, whereas video editors lack the paired data to learn them. papers.title: Improving and Expanding Video Editing Capabilities Without Videos
papers.tldr: I2VT transfers image-editing capabilities to video editors using only single images, improving existing tasks and enabling new edits while preserving temporal consistency.

papers.abstract: Guidance repels the prediction of a diffusion model away from a weaker reference prediction. It substantially improves sample quality, but its mechanism remains poorly understood. We first find that, at the scales used in practice, guidance does not improve the prediction of the posterior mean (the model's training target); it makes the prediction worse, while samples improve. Second, posterior-mean predictions have less variance than the data, and we find that guidance restores it. We introduce variance-matched guidance: a closed-form rule that picks the guidance scale by matching the variance of the guided predictions to that of the data. Without tuning, it recovers the hand-picked scales of eleven widely used models across image, video, audio, motion, and world generation; to our knowledge, no previous explanation of guidance predicts them. Applied per noise level, it yields a schedule without tuned hyperparameters that users prefer to hand-crafted ones on SD 3.5 Medium. Third, we offer an interpretation of the mechanism behind guidance: each model makes a random error in predicting the posterior mean, and guidance rescales the difference of these errors into a sample with the posterior's covariance, which improves sampling. This view also suggests two new hypotheses that our experiments support: guidance can work with negative scales, and guiding a model with its own checkpoint needs a larger scale than guiding it with an independently trained model.
authors: Ali Backour, Artem Lukoianov, Frank Permenter, Tommi Jaakkola, Justin Solomon, Vincent Sitzmann
bullets: Guidance can worsen posterior-mean prediction even as it improves generated samples.
Variance-matched guidance selects scales by matching guided-prediction variance to the data variance.
The rule recovers hand-tuned scales across image, video, audio, motion, and world-generation models.
Applied across noise levels, it produces an untuned schedule preferred over handcrafted schedules on SD 3.5 Medium.
The error-based interpretation supports guidance with negative scales and explains why self-guidance needs larger scales.

papers.abstract: Poetry-to-video generation requires more than translating text into visual scenes. Poetic language is highly compressed, often depends on historical and cultural knowledge, and frequently conveys meaning through metaphor, imagery, and other non-literal expressions. We introduce PoVi, a benchmark and agentic framework for grounded poetry-to-video generation, evaluating semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization. PoVi reconstructs poem semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively transforms them into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans, followed by narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, PoVi consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations. PoVi provides a testbed for studying knowledge-grounded, long-horizon multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.

papers.abstract: Generative video models are becoming powerful renderers, yet lack the predictable control interfaces of conventional systems such as HTML/CSS engines or Blender. Their capabilities emerge implicitly from training, making it difficult to determine what they can reliably execute. We present Neural Rendering Compiler (NeurCo), which automatically probes frozen video models to construct model-specific capability manuals describing which semantic requirements they can reliably satisfy. NeurCo represents user intent in a model-agnostic intermediate representation of objects, constraints, events, and cameras, then compiles it into model-specific execution strategies. Reliable requirements remain unchanged, while unreliable ones are selectively rewritten or compiled into alternative execution strategies. We introduce VComBench, a benchmark of 380 compositional, multi-requirement tasks spanning text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video generation. NeurCo improves requirement satisfaction from 46.8% to 52.3% on Wan and from 66.5% to 69.3% on Minimax H3, and achieves further gains when combined with prompt enhancers, including on Seedance 2.5. Our analysis reveals model-specific differences in control capabilities and trade-offs between controllability and photorealism, highlighting capability-guided compilation as a promising approach to programmable generative video rendering.

papers.abstract: Recent video generators produce realistic videos, yet controlling how scenes unfold remains challenging. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, guide generation by specifying scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order. However, these coarse inputs leave details unspecified and may contain artifacts that should not be reproduced. Successful proxy-guided generation must therefore Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and Bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events. We introduce ProxyGenBench to study these interacting requirements, with 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across three scene tasks and controlled variations in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. We evaluate five video generators using verified, case-specific checklists. Experiments show that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but greater proxy detail can coincide with poorer completion, while strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding.

papers.abstract: Modern video generators excel at producing visually plausible futures guided by text and image prompts. Yet their emphasis on semantic plausibility does not guarantee fidelity to the physical consequences of specific actions. Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), in contrast, aim to simulate how the world responds to robot actions, enabling scalable policy evaluation and improvement without costly real-world rollouts. The challenge is not merely to generate a plausible future, but to predict what follows from a specific physical action. As video priors grow stronger, we ask how little adaptation is truly needed to bridge this gap. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal recipe that preserves and unlocks the capabilities of strong video priors through unified physical action conditioning, training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout, and thus the consequences of actions, are decided, and native history conditioning. Built upon MiniMax H3, a 33B video foundation model, Dianjing freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only 0.34% of its parameters using approximately 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, without additional robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Controlled ablations show that where training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network. On WorldOracle, which evaluates predictions against paired real-world executions, Dianjing achieves the best scores on four of the five evaluation tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long. Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models aim to predict future interactions that are both visually realistic and physically consistent. Yet explicit 3D motion prediction alone does not guarantee that object structure and contact relationships are preserved. Beyond motion prediction, 3D representations provide an explicit state space for imposing structural and physical constraints. Building on this insight, we introduce RehearsalWorld, an editable robot world model driven by 3D Interaction Rehearsal (3DIR). Given an initial RGB-D observation and robot actions, Interaction-Consistent Rehearsal (ICR) uses a pretrained 3D point-flow model as a motion prior. It refines the predicted trajectories through response-aware object grouping, persistent grasp memory, and contact structure refiner, preserving scene stability, object structure, and grasp attachments. Rehearsal-Aligned Video Generation (RAVG) then uses geometric projections of the rehearsal as temporal conditioning. We fine-tune a video generator on projection-video pairs to synthesize realistic interaction videos. Thanks to the decoupling of physical response from visual synthesis, RehearsalWorld also supports independent editing of material properties and camera viewpoints. Compared with PointWorld on real DROID grasping sequences, RehearsalWorld reduces gripper-relative offset by approximately 79% to 84% across deformable, articulated, and rigid objects and lowers reference motion error. For video prediction, it achieves a PSNR of 23.92 dB and an FVD of 149.
authors: Guangyu Liu, Hanzhang Wang, Huijia Zhang, Hanbei Zhan, Linjie Hu, Bin Xiao, Xuan Zhou, Dong Zhang, Hanwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the gap between explicit 3D motion prediction and preserving object structure, contacts, and grasp relationships.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce EiT by exploring the key design factors of pixel-space diffusion from three perspectives: model architecture, representation, and frequency domain. Inspired by Denoising Autoencoders (DAE) which perform denoising through a bottleneck, we construct a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer that performs explicit compression along the channel dimension. In terms of representation, we find that both pixel and latent diffusion transformers exhibit a three-stage representation dynamics across layers and timesteps: denoising/local feature expansion, basis lift-up, and posterior projection. Moreover, earlier denoising and a longer basis lift-up stage are associated with better generation, which EiT naturally achieves through its channel bottleneck and increased network depth. From the frequency perspective, we establish the equivalence between pixel-space and frequency-space diffusion when keeping the network operating in pixel space. On ImageNet $256\times256$ and $512\times512$, EiT consistently outperforms JiT (Just image Transformers) in generation quality. Specifically, our EiT achieves better FID than JiT: 1.61 vs. 1.85 at $256\times256$, and 1.73 vs. 1.99 at $512\times512$. Remarkably, EiT can be seamlessly applied to video pixel diffusion by simply extending the patch size to temporal dimension and outperforms video latent diffusion in FVD evaluated on Kinetics-600 (resolution 256), under comparable total network parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/forever208/EiT
authors: Mang Ning, Le Zhang, Albert Ali Salah, Itir Onal Ertugrul, Jintao Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Pixel-space diffusion design involves interacting architectural, representation, and frequency-domain factors.
Method: EiT uses a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer with explicit channel-wise compression inspired by denoising autoencoders.

Finding: Diffusion representations progress through denoising/local feature expansion, basis lift-up, and posterior projection; earlier denoising and longer basis lift-up correlate with better generation.
Result: EiT achieves lower FID than JiT on ImageNet at 256×256 and 512×512, and outperforms video latent diffusion in FVD on Kinetics-600 under comparable parameter counts.
Scope: The same approach extends to video by enlarging patch size along the temporal dimension.

papers.abstract: We present SPARC, a geometry-guided attention pruning framework that turns the native self-attention of pretrained video diffusion transformers into a unified mechanism for camera control and persistent scene memory. Our key insight is that attention connectivity can simultaneously serve as geometric conditioning for camera control and spatial addressing for historical memory retrieval. Motivated by the asymmetric contextual requirements of reconstructing observed content and synthesizing novel regions, SPARC restricts observed tokens to geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context, while preserving dense attention for unobserved regions. Correspondence-aware attention biasing and order-invariant historical positioning further enable stable retrieval across long temporal gaps. Without introducing additional learnable control or memory modules, SPARC achieves precise camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation while substantially reducing attention computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of aggressive attention pruning in improving camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity, with an inference speedup of over 50x when combined with four-step distillation. Project page is available at https://zju3dv.github.io/SPARC.
authors: Zesong Yang, Weikai Chen, Liyuan Cui, Yuan Li, Jiaxin Huang, Lutao Jiang, Runze Zhang, Yingda Yin, Xiaoyang Huang, Kai Yan, Keyang Luo, Xin Wang, Hujun Bao, Zhaopeng Cui
bullets: Addresses camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation in long-horizon camera-controlled video generation.
Uses geometric correspondences to guide attention and retrieve relevant historical scene content.
Restricts observed regions to matching historical tokens plus local context, while retaining dense attention for novel regions.
Adds correspondence-aware attention biases and order-invariant historical positioning for stable retrieval across long temporal gaps.
Reports improved camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity while substantially reducing attention computation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. System Overview. For each target chunk, SPARC establishes token-level correspondences with historical observations through local geometric projection, and then prunes the backbone’s native self-attention to focus on geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context for previously observed regions, while newly revealed regions retain dense attention for flexible content synthesis. Historical RoPE re-indexing is employed to eliminate artificial temporal ordering biases among retrieved historical observations. The generated observations are subsequently appended to the history bank for continuous rollout.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on DL3DV-Eval. Given the same input image and camera trajectory, we show frames generated with different methods along the roaming time. Explicit-3D baselines drift from the target trajectory or accumulate geometric distortions, and implicit baselines fail to follow the prescribed camera path, whereas SPARC preserves scene appearance and accurate camera control throughout the rollout. See Supp. for additional scenes and video comparisons.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of revisitation on WorldScore-Static. Each scene follows a closed-loop camera trajectory (top view), and frames are sampled along the roaming time. Baselines either distort the scene or fail to recover the originally observed content upon revisiting, whereas our SPARC faithfully restores the scene at both revisits. See Supp. for additional scenes and video comparisons.

Figure 9. Additional long-horizon generation results. Without any degradation-aware augmentation, SPARC generates high-fidelity, minute-long videos with precise camera adherence and persistent scene consistency.

Figure 7. Ablation on attention pruning and historical RoPE indexing. Progressively incorporating geometric correspondence, local window attention, and correspondence bias improves camera adherence and reconstruction fidelity. The bottom rows visualize the pixel-wise difference |∆| between outputs generated using the original and shuffled history orders: sequential history RoPE yields discrepancies that grow along the trajectory, whereas our shared indexing remains invariant.

Figure 2. Redundancy of dense full self-attention. Most target regions have been observed in historical frames and require only sparse geometric correspondences for faithful reconstruction, while newly revealed regions benefit from broader contextual interactions.
Figure 8. Attention weight visualization. Given target queries, dense attention with the camera adapter exhibits attention peaks that deviate from geometrically corresponding historical regions.
Figure 5. Camera alignment. SPARC achieves the best camera alignment on DL3DV-Evaluation.

Figure 10. Training-free dynamic scene generation. We segment the foreground object and shift its correspondence locations along a prescribed motion trajectory, allowing SPARC to synthesize natural object motion consistent with the specified trajectory.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models for game interaction and control have increased the demand for large-scale gameplay videos paired with camera trajectories. However, capturing synchronized camera trajectories often requires game-specific pipelines, limiting scalability. We therefore propose GameWeaver, a unified diffusion framework that automatically produces paired video--camera data through three complementary tasks: camera pose estimation from observed video, video generation along a prescribed camera trajectory, and joint video--camera generation from a reference image and text. First, each tipxel stores the normalized 3D coordinates of a pixel ray's endpoint in a reference coordinate frame. The resulting three-channel tipxel fields and RGB frames share the pretrained video model's VAE. Next, a fully trainable dual-stream Transformer exchanges appearance and geometry features through bidirectional gated attention and conditions both streams on shared text features. Finally, deterministic fitting recovers camera intrinsics and normalized trajectories from generated tipxel fields. In our evaluation tasks, GameWeaver achieves a normalized translation MSE of 0.0029 for camera control; for joint generation, it scores 85.48 out of 100 on instruction adherence versus 64.71 for the best cascade on that metric, validating the feasibility of the proposed approach.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yifan Huang, Jixuan Zhang, Peifeng Wang, Yuying Ma, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses the scalability challenge of collecting synchronized gameplay videos and camera trajectories with game-specific pipelines.
Represents geometry using three-channel tipxel fields sharing a pretrained video model’s VAE with RGB frames.
Uses a dual-stream Transformer with bidirectional gated attention and shared text conditioning.
Supports camera-pose estimation, trajectory-conditioned video generation, and joint video–camera generation from an image and text.
Reports 0.0029 normalized translation MSE for camera control and 85.48/100 instruction adherence for joint generation, compared with 64.71 for the best cascade.

figures.caption: Figure 1. One diffusion model for three tasks. Pose estimation predicts cameras from video and text. Camera control generates video from a reference image, a given trajectory, and text. Joint generation predicts video and cameras from a reference image and text. TARGET marks predicted outputs and GIVEN marks observed inputs. The resulting pairs support camera-conditioned world-model training.

Figure 4. Qualitative results across tasks. (a) Pose estimation on Minecraft videos. The right-hand panels compare estimated and ground-truth (GT) cameras. (b) Camera control generates CF videos from reference frames along specified paths. (c) Joint generation produces CS:GO videos and camera trajectories from reference images and text. Frusta show camera poses along each trajectory.

Figure 2. Training and inference with RGB and tipxel maps. (a) Training fixes the known latents and interpolates noise separately in each stream. Velocity supervision covers the unknown elements Ω, with |Ω|= M in Eq. 5. At inference, the frozen VAE decodes sampled latents. Fitting the decoded tipxel maps yields rotations, normalized translations, and intrinsics. Pose estimation retains the observed RGB frames. (b) Bidirectional attention and zero-initialized residual gates couple the streams in each DiT block. Projected text c supplies keys and values to both text cross-attention layers. The streams share self-attention and text-attention weights within each block, with separate feed-forward networks and output heads. Flames mark trainable weights, snowflakes frozen weights, and locks fixed conditions.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion and world models generate plausible videos but do not reliably match the requested camera direction and travel distance. We present DreamTour, a training-free framework that generates camera tours from a single image with more accurate control over camera motion. DreamTour first uses a frozen image inpainting prior to extend the photograph beyond its original field of view while preserving the input pixels. Depth-based rendering of this extended scene along the requested camera path produces approximate target views that serve as spatial guidance. We introduce Layout Steering, which aligns early video latents with these views through decaying low-frequency corrections, leaving later denoising to refine appearance and dynamics. For longer tours, we autoregressively generate the video segments, repeating guidance construction from each segment's final frame to maintain camera control across the full trajectory. DreamTour improves directional accuracy and travel calibration on VBench while maintaining competitive video quality. On WorldScore, it strengthens camera control and scene consistency across chained movements. Together, these results demonstrate that training-free spatial guidance enables more accurate and consistent camera control in pretrained video diffusion and world models.
authors: Srikumar Sastry, Meher Gitika Karumuri, Chenqi Li, Sarosij Bose, Mellon Zhang, Allen Tu, Ziyang Long, Yen-Liang Lin, Alexander Schwing, Nathan Jacobs
bullets: Extends the input image beyond its field of view using a frozen inpainting prior while preserving original pixels.
Renders depth-based views along the desired camera path to provide spatial guidance.
Uses Layout Steering to apply decaying low-frequency corrections early in denoising, then lets later steps refine video appearance and dynamics.
Autoregressively chains segments for longer tours, rebuilding guidance from each segment’s final frame.
Improves directional accuracy, travel calibration, camera control, and scene consistency on VBench and WorldScore while maintaining competitive video quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DreamTour. (a) A frozen inpainting model expands the input image into a canvas. Figure 3. Canvas and guide construction. A frozen inpainting prior expands the input image while preserving its pixels exactly. Estimated depth lifts the canvas into a textured 3D point cloud, rendered along the requested camera path to form a guide video.

Figure 10. Qualitative camera control across eight requested motions. Additional CamProbe-protocol examples complement Figure 4 of the main paper. Figure 8. Why net camera travel must be measured. (a) Sim(3) fitting can rescale a nearly stationary trajectory and reduce translation error, while small per-step rotations can make a stationary view appear favorable under RPE-R. (b) Our unaligned metricscale evaluation projects net camera displacement onto the requested direction. Off-axis travel does not contribute to the travel ratio and is measured separately through direction error θ.

The dashed line indicates requested travel (r = 1), and the shaded band marks r ∈ [0.75, 1.25]. The displayed range is clipped to [−2, 4]. Wide and asymmetric distributions explain why median travel error and the fraction within ±25% of the requested distance provide complementary summaries. Rotation ratios are evaluated separately.

Table 2. Camera control and video quality under the CamProbe [15] protocol. We evaluate eight camera motions on VBench [17] using Depth Anything 3 [23] poses. RPE-T and RPE-R measure raw relative translation and rotation errors without trajectory alignment or scale fitting. Dir. measures mean angular error in net motion. Travel and rotation errors report median |r − 1|, where r is realized motion along the requested direction. Quality metrics assess imaging, smoothness, and background consistency. The training column indicates whether the method requires camera-control training beyond its base video prior. Layout Steering adds no training, including when applied to already camera-conditioned world models.

The shaded rows mark the selected configuration, with weight 1.5 applied over the first 50% of denoising with linear decay. Camera errors are lower-is-better, while quality scores are higher-is-better.

Table 9. Layout Steering ablation on Lyra 2.0. Evaluated on 24 synthetic FLUX.3 scenes with eight camera motions per scene. The model retains its native trajectory conditioning in every setting. Table 5. Ablation of Layout Steering on 24 synthetic FLUX.3 scenes [5]. We evaluate Wan 2.2 [31] on eight camera motions per scene following the protocol in Table 2. Full-frequency steering yields the lowest motion errors but introduces visible artifacts. Alternative guides and schedules compromise control or background consistency. Shaded rows mark DreamTour’s selected configuration.
Table 3. Camera control and consistency on WorldScore [10]. The static split has 2,000 single-image worlds with one or three camera movements. Best results in each group are bold.

Table 6. Perceptual quality of newly revealed content. We evaluate MUSIQ [19] and CLIP-IQA [33] on newly revealed image bands from the scenes in Table 5. Decaying low-frequency steering scores highest on both metrics.

Values are mean ± standard deviation over the observed clips, with n pooled across repeated seeds. Positive lateral camera travel is leftward and positive vertical travel is upward. papers.abstract: Attention over long sequences is a major computational bottleneck in video generation, which can be alleviated through sparsity and low-bit quantization. We propose JetDiffusion, a video generation system built on trainable Video Sparse Quantized Attention (VSQA), with custom inference kernels that combine native NVFP4 computation and kernel fusion. At 90% sparsity, VSQA accelerates attention by 8-29x compared with FlashAttention on different hardwares. To further accelerate video generation, we combine VSQA with NVFP4 linear quantization and step distillation. Although each technique can individually preserve generation quality, jointly adapting to all three remains challenging, particularly under aggressive NVFP4 quantization. Through empirical studies, we develop an effective staged training recipe that enables stable adaptation to quantization, sparsity, and few-step denoising. On Wan2.1-14B, the resulting model achieves 273x end-to-end video generation speedup on the RTX 5090 while maintaining comparable video quality.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate sequences by progressively unmasking tokens, but errors introduced during decoding are typically irreversible. Recent work has shown that iterative correction can improve sample quality, yet existing theory fails to explain this given a learned, imperfect denoiser model. We re-formulate MDM inference as a Markov chain on the clean sequence space, defined by a remask-denoise kernel that randomly re-introduces masks and then denoises. This helps us analyze the actual denoising trajectory towards the data distribution. The analysis motivates Random Remask-Denoise (R$^2$D) inference, a purely test-time, finetuning-free, reward-free procedure. To further improve performance, we propose Trajectory Correction Training (TCT), a denoiser-training procedure that exposes the model to its own errors along the generation trajectory. On logical tasks, our approach exhibits a striking near-log-linear test-time scaling, achieving over 97% accuracy on hard Sudoku puzzles and over 99% accuracy on 3-SAT. Our approach also applies to pretrained models on actual language tasks, beating iterative correction baselines and the official Q-mode accuracy of LLaDA2.1-mini on HumanEval+.
bullets: Masked diffusion decoding errors are usually irreversible, limiting generation quality.
The paper models inference as a Markov chain using a remask-denoise kernel that randomly re-masks tokens before denoising.
This analysis motivates Random Remask-Denoise (R²D), a finetuning-free, reward-free, test-time method.
Trajectory Correction Training (TCT) trains denoisers on errors encountered during their own generation trajectories.
On logical tasks, the approach achieves over 97% Sudoku accuracy and over 99% 3-SAT accuracy, and improves pretrained-model results on language tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generative models have enabled flexible conditional generation and editing pipelines, such as text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-guided synthesis. However, these workflows are inherently one-directional, mapping conditions to videos without providing a mechanism to invert this process. In complex media production settings, the ability to recover controllable textual conditions from a given video is highly desirable, yet remains underexplored. While inverse prompting has been studied for image generation, directly extending these approaches to video is challenging due to the need to capture temporal dynamics beyond static appearance, as well as the substantial computational cost of per-video optimization. In this work, we propose the first practical framework for efficient video inverse prompting. Specifically, we formulate inverse prompting as a meta-learning problem and introduce Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta-prompt optimized over temporal dimensions to enable fast and effective prompt inference. Our approach amortizes the inversion process, eliminating the need for costly iterative optimization at test time. Experimental results demonstrate that MVIP recovers higher-quality inverse prompts with significantly improved reconstruction fidelity compared to image-based inversion and iterative captioning baselines, while achieving substantial gains in efficiency. Code and video results are available at https://ueriniuno.github.io/mvip-page/.
bullets: Addresses the lack of methods for inverting video-generation pipelines to recover controllable text conditions.
Introduces Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta-prompt optimized across temporal dimensions.
Amortizes inversion, eliminating iterative per-video optimization at inference time.
Reports higher-quality inverse prompts, better reconstruction fidelity, and improved efficiency than image-based inversion and iterative captioning baselines.
Focuses on capturing video temporal dynamics beyond static appearance.

papers.abstract: Creating a dialogue scene typically requires cutting between multiple views (e.g., close-ups, medium shots, and over-the-shoulder shots) of the actors. Yet capturing such coverage is costly and in many settings unavailable. We study dialogue re-cinematography: synthesizing additional shots from a single wide-angle dialogue video. Existing video generators can synthesize new shots, but rely on visual cues alone, so when the source video barely shows the lips, the generated lip motion fails to match the speech. Our key observation is that the speech audio is view-invariant: it constrains lip motion in any target view. Building on this insight, we adapt a pretrained audio-visual diffusion model to generate the new shot from a target frame that specifies the view, a source video that contains the performance, and the speech audio that drives lip motion. In multi-person scenes, however, pretrained audio-visual models drive every visible face with the same speech, causing speech leakage, where silent listeners mouth the speaker's words. We therefore introduce speaker-aware audio gating, a training-free module that lets the audio drive only the faces that speak in the target shot. On a cinematic paired-view benchmark spanning diverse viewpoints and framings, our method lowers perceptual error by 59%, landmark error by 56%, and speech leakage by 97% relative to the strongest baseline, Wan 3.0. Our method also remains robust on in-the-wild scenes, highlighting its potential for film post-production.
authors: Anthony Chen, Naomi Ken Korem, Matan Ben-Yosef, Tavi Halperin, Urska Jelercic, Ofir Bibi, Daniel Cohen-Or, Or Patashnik, Maneesh Agrawala
bullets: Addresses the costly or unavailable multi-camera coverage needed for dialogue scenes.
Adapts a pretrained audio-visual diffusion model using a target frame for composition, source video for performance, and speech audio for lip motion.
Introduces training-free speaker-aware audio gating to prevent speech leakage onto silent listeners.
On a paired-view cinematic benchmark, reduces perceptual error by 59%, landmark error by 56%, and speech leakage by 97% versus Wan 3.0.
Also shows robustness on in-the-wild scenes, supporting potential film post-production use.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Method overview. From a source video with its speech audio, a target frame of the desired shot, and its shot prompt, our audio-visual diffusion model generates the synchronized target-view video. Right: speaker-aware audio gating. To prevent silent listeners from mouthing the speaker’s words (speech leakage), an active-speaker detector labels each face in the source as speaking or silent. papers.abstract: Event cameras capture asynchronous brightness changes at high temporal resolution, but scarce recordings constrain data-driven research. Sparse RGB observations cannot uniquely determine intervening events since identical frames may correspond to streams with different activity, polarities, and timing. Existing simulators largely rely on prescribed sensor dynamics and estimated brightness trajectories, whose assumptions limit the diversity and fidelity of plausible event streams. We introduce EventDiffusion, a hierarchical generative framework that directly learns the conditional distribution of native asynchronous event streams from real recordings. EventDiffusion decomposes generation into three probabilistic processes: Event Activity Diffusion (EAD) learns stochastic discrete event counts; Event Spatial Allocation (ESA) distributes these counts to individual pixels while preserving cardinality; and Event Timing Diffusion (ETD) learns continuous asynchronous timestamp distributions. We also introduce CEFS, an event-stream realism metric combining event activity and polarity with multiscale space-time structure and temporal fidelity. Across all datasets, EventDiffusion achieves double the accuracy of SOTA methods and demonstrates robustness across different cameras at any resolution.
authors: Karthik Sundar Senthilkumar, Christopher Thirgood, Simon Hadfield
bullets: Sparse RGB frames cannot uniquely recover the intervening events’ activity, polarity, and timing.
Event Activity Diffusion models discrete event counts, Event Spatial Allocation assigns them to pixels, and Event Timing Diffusion predicts continuous timestamps.
CEFS evaluates realism using activity, polarity, multiscale space-time structure, and temporal fidelity.
The method reportedly achieves twice the accuracy of prior state-of-the-art methods and remains robust across cameras and resolutions.

papers.abstract: Multi-frame video frame interpolation (VFI) aims to reconstruct dense video from sparse keyframes, requiring accurate intermediate motion and faithful appearance. As temporal gaps grow, flow-based methods can retain observed textures but misplace them under ambiguous motion, whereas iterative latent-diffusion models can synthesize plausible content but incur substantial sampling costs and may alter details during reconstruction with a variational autoencoder (VAE). We present RePix-VFI, named for Re-rendering observed Pixels, a multi-frame VFI framework that couples draft-conditioned one-step video diffusion with reconstruction from observed keyframes. A pretrained video diffusion model refines a flow-rendered draft of the whole window in a single forward pass. For each target frame, our generative readback matches its two bounding keyframes to the generated prediction using an optical-flow estimator. The resulting correspondences guide re-rendering of original keyframe RGB pixels outside the VAE. A lightweight appearance fusion head combines these renderings with generated appearance. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction and perceptual quality. On SNU-FILM at $\times$8 and $\times$16, RePix-VFI achieves the highest PSNR and the lowest LPIPS, FloLPIPS, and tOF among the compared methods, exceeding the best evaluated diffusion-based baseline by 1.71 and 1.48dB in PSNR, respectively. It also runs 32--42$\times$ faster than the state-of-the-art multi-frame VFI diffusion model.
authors: Dayeon Kim, Jeonghyeok Do, Munchurl Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving keyframe details while estimating ambiguous motion across large temporal gaps.
Refines a flow-rendered draft of the full video window with a pretrained one-step video diffusion model.
Matches generated frames to bounding keyframes via optical flow, then re-renders original RGB pixels outside the VAE.
Uses a lightweight fusion head to combine re-rendered keyframe appearance with generated content.
On SNU-FILM at ×8 and ×16, achieves the best reported PSNR and perceptual metrics among compared methods, while running 32–42× faster than a leading multi-frame VFI diffusion model.

papers.abstract: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after a switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), a simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with a correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from a single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines.
authors: NaHyeon Park, Kyeong-Hwan Moon, Youjin Jeon, Hyunjung Shim
bullets: Streaming models exhibit context inertia: previous video chunks can overpower newly changed prompts.
Discarding or editing cached context risks breaking visual continuity, even when only the previous chunk is retained.
RG measures a cache-free residual by denoising the re-noised previous chunk under the new prompt, then applies it early in generation of the next chunk.
The training-free method improves prompt switching across single- and multi-switch settings while largely preserving visual quality.
It adds one forward pass per chunk and requires no per-model tuning, enabling integration into existing pipelines.

papers.abstract: Sol-Attn (Sparsifying online attention) combines sparse exact computation with low-cost representative approximation to accelerate training-free inference in diffusion video models. However, intra-block attention can focus on only a few tokens. While preserving these key interactions exactly, the block-level decision incurs the cost of evaluating many low-response members. We propose Sol$^{3}$, a training-free hierarchical sparse attention method that further refines how exact computations are allocated. First, we introduce Gaussian-guided hierarchical routing, which determines the scope of exact computation step by step, from blocks to tokens, using statistical thresholds at each level. Only a subset of members within Mixed blocks that require refinement is selected for exact computation, while representative terms approximate the remaining members. We further design heterogeneous routing statistics that combine block-center correlations with variations in Key and Value within blocks to identify blocks that are difficult to approximate. Among these Mixed blocks, we uniformly compare raw token relevance to select members requiring exact computation. Experiments on video generation, audio-video co-generation, and world simulation tasks demonstrate that Sol$^{3}$ achieves 86% attention sparsity and delivers a $3.07\times$ attention speedup while preserving quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/FofGofx/sol3.
authors: Guoxin Fan, Weilun Feng, Chuanguang Yang, Mingqiang Wu, Xiaokun Liu, Jitao Lu, Zhulin An, Libo Huang, Boyu Diao, Di Gao, Yongjun Xu
bullets: Motivation: block-level sparse attention can waste computation on low-response tokens even when only a few intra-block interactions matter.
Method: Gaussian-guided hierarchical routing narrows exact computation from blocks to selected tokens, while representative approximations handle the rest.
Routing uses block-center correlations plus Key/Value variation to identify blocks that are difficult to approximate.
Experiments across video generation, audio-video co-generation, and world simulation report 86% attention sparsity and a 3.07× attention speedup while preserving quality.
Scope: the method is training-free and targets attention computation in diffusion video models.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.
authors: Zhilu Zhang, Xiaoyu Liu, Wenxi Liu, Shengfeng He
bullets: Addresses the mutation or disappearance of moving objects after they leave and re-enter the camera view.
Couples perspective video generation with low-frame-rate panoramic evolution without auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs.
Uses Geometric Anchoring for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation for temporal aggregation.
Supports both latent-level and attention-level camera conditioning architectures.
Experiments on a new dynamic benchmark show gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the OmniPersist framework. Tokens from the dense perspective stream and the temporally sparse panoramic stream are jointly processed by a shared, frozen Diffusion Transformer (DiT) block adapted via LoRA. The two streams coordinate across space and time via dedicated learned feature projections to exchange complementary context. GeoAnch transfers spatially aligned features at synchronized timestamps, while TemComp aggregates features across neighboring timestamps for intermediate observations. For illustration, we depict a temporal sampling interval of s = 4 in image-space indices.

Figure 3. Generation results on I2V across camera revisits. From top to bottom, we show a frame before the camera turns away and two revisit frames after it returns to illustrate identity preservation and continued motion. papers.abstract: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).
authors: Joonghyuk Shin, Alex Trevithick, Katar\'ina T\'othov\'a, Liyuan Zhu, Shengyu Huang, Jaesik Park, Shalini De Mello, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Riccardo de Lutio, Haithem Turki
bullets: Video world models often lose long-term visual consistency, while explicit 3D worlds lack photorealistic appearance.
M2R stores rendered features on mesh surfaces in each object’s coordinate frame and retrieves them by rasterizing visible surfaces.
This makes appearance move with objects, persist across revisits, and remain shared among observing agents, with memory tied to surfaces rather than frames.
Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and coding-agent-authored worlds.
It more than doubles object permanence, nearly doubles cross-agent consistency, and renders 720p video at 40 FPS.

When agent B encounters the same surfaces, it retrieves and renders them as agent A saw them (a). We train our renderer on rollouts that revisit earlier views. With a one-chunk window, it must render each revisit from the memory it wrote, supervised by a frozen teacher that sees the full past (b).

papers.abstract: Long-horizon panoramic video wandering aims to continuously synthesize scene-consistent $360^\circ$ observations along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial equirectangular projection (ERP) panorama. Existing panoramic video models have achieved promising results in camera-controlled generation, while recent 3D-guided approaches further provide geometric guidance for improving scene consistency. However, stable long-horizon wandering remains challenging due to diverse motion--orientation relationships and imperfect memory guidance induced by accumulated generation artifacts and depth inaccuracies. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PVWander}, a 3D-memory-guided framework that accumulates generated observations into an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide subsequent generation, with two complementary designs: \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} for motion--orientation alignment and \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} for adaptive memory guidance. \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} exploits the horizontal cyclic symmetry of ERP panoramas to uniformly align each clip's ERP orientation with its principal translation direction, yielding more consistent, forward-like relative motions while preserving the prescribed camera path. \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} exploits the coarse-to-fine nature of diffusion denoising to adaptively regulate reprojected memory guidance through timestep-dependent channel-wise gates, preserving its structural benefits while mitigating visual artifacts from imperfect projections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PVWander achieves improved long-horizon generation quality, while ablations validate the effectiveness of both designs.
authors: Chuanxin Song, Xiaodong Wang, Shijie Chen, Junliang Xie, Zhanmi Zhong, Suiying Wu, Peixi Peng
bullets: Targets scene-consistent panoramic video synthesis along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial ERP panorama.
Accumulates generated observations in an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide future frames.
Path-Facing canonicalization aligns ERP orientation with the principal translation direction while preserving the camera path.
Timestep-aware gating adaptively controls memory guidance during diffusion denoising to reduce artifacts from imperfect projections.
Experiments and ablations report improved long-horizon generation quality and validate both design components.

papers.abstract: Automatic visual story generation using diffusion-based models has become an increasingly important research direction in generative artificial intelligence. However, maintaining character identity consistency across consecutive frames remains an open challenge, as existing models often produce significant variations in facial traits, clothing, visual style, or anatomical proportions. This paper proposes a modular pipeline to improve character identity consistency in multi-frame visual story generation using Stable Diffusion XL alongside additional conditioning and automatic selection mechanisms. The proposed system integrates LoRA fine-tuning for character personalization, ControlNet for pose-based structural control, and IP-Adapter for visual identity transfer. Furthermore, a reranking mechanism based on Best-of-K candidate selection and persistent identity memory is introduced to automatically select the most visually consistent generated images. The work also includes integrating and extending the StoryDiffusion framework into a reproducible local workflow, along with improvements for generated frame selection. Performance evaluation uses automatic metrics such as CLIP image similarity, DINO similarity, and CLIP text-image alignment. Experimental evaluation was conducted on a custom benchmark of multiple characters and visual stories organized into difficulty levels (easy, medium, and difficult). Both progressive variants of the proposed pipeline and extended versions of StoryDiffusion were evaluated, including SDXL baseline, Best-of-K, Identity Memory, and the Full Pipeline. Results show that reranking, identity memory, and visual conditioning reduce identity drift across frames and improve the overall coherence and stability of generated visual stories.

CLIP, DINO, and text-image alignment results indicate improved identity consistency and story coherence, though the evaluation is limited to the custom benchmark and tested configurations.

papers.abstract: Generating videos with physically plausible dynamics remains challenging despite advances in visual quality. Latent world models offer predictive signals for evaluating physical plausibility, but higher agreement between predicted and observed features may reflect easier-to-predict scene content rather than more plausible dynamics. We propose \textbf{S}elf-Referenced \textbf{P}hysical \textbf{A}lignment \textbf{R}ewards (\textbf{SPAR}), a framework that uses world-model predictions for inference-time physical alignment. SPAR compares each video's prediction error with that of static clips constructed by repeating its own frames, providing a content-matched reference for evaluating generated dynamics. To account for the uneven spatial and temporal distribution of physical interactions, we introduce a unified \textbf{spatiotemporal reward refinement} strategy. \textbf{Spatial refinement} emphasizes localized prediction discrepancies, while \textbf{temporal refinement} moderates brief error peaks and supplements prediction errors with agreement between predicted and observed feature changes. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that SPAR improves the physical plausibility of both \textbf{text-to-video generation} and \textbf{image-to-video continuation}, bringing generated dynamics into closer alignment with the physical regularities governing real-world events. Additional results and resources are available at https://gavin-jy.github.io/spar-page/
authors: Junyi Zhang, Qichao Wang, Wenzhe Qian, Yuanchuan Wang, Min Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge that world-model prediction agreement can reflect predictable content rather than physically plausible dynamics.
Compares a video's prediction error with static, frame-repeated clips from the same video to create a content-matched reference.
Uses spatial refinement to focus on localized interactions and temporal refinement to reduce sensitivity to brief error spikes.
Adds agreement between predicted and observed feature changes to complement prediction-error signals.
Evaluations across multiple benchmarks show improved physical plausibility for both text-to-video and image-to-video generation.

papers.abstract: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at https://zengkaiya.github.io/Loupe/.
authors: Kai Zeng, Ruichuan An, Zhen Fang, Xi Fang, Han Lyu, Moran Li, Yingchen Yu, Yifan Dai, Bohan Zeng, Quanqing Xu, Zhengzhou Zhu, Wentao Zhang

Improves evaluation across three video generators; MiniMax-H3’s overall score rises from 32.80 to 70.67, with further gains on scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness.

papers.abstract: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).
authors: Jian Yang, Zhizhuo Kou, Qiyuan Zhu, Han Chen, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Persistent clean-KV updates can dominate runtime once denoising is accelerated, while stale-cache reuse increases later denoising work.
SAMR combines motion-aligned historical KV with in-flight KV, using calibrated affine correction and selective true $t=0$ refreshes.
Tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels implement the reconstruction efficiently without retraining the frozen video DiT.
On LongLive-1.3B, it cuts DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7%, while improving final-quarter PSNR over token reuse.
It transfers to Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B, reducing reuse-induced step inflation and improving late-stage PSNR, with calibration further recovering diagnostic quality.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation requires predicting how robot-object interactions evolve over time, encompassing both visual appearance and scene geometry. In multi-camera settings, such predictions need to capture the evolving 3D scene consistently across viewpoints, while supporting controllable generation under different robot actions and camera configurations. Existing video generation models provide strong priors for visual appearance and motion but typically lack explicit geometric modeling. Meanwhile, recent advances in geometry-aware and multi-view generation have explored joint appearance-geometry modeling and cross-view consistency, yet generating temporally coherent appearance and geometry across multiple viewpoints under robotic manipulation conditions remains challenging. In this work, we propose GeoMVGen, a framework for joint multi-view RGB and pointmap video generation in robotic manipulation. Built on a video diffusion transformer, our framework employs modality-specific adaptation modules to capture the distinct characteristics of appearance and geometry, while using cross-modal residual connections to facilitate information exchange between the two modalities. To establish geometric correspondences across viewpoints, we further introduce a cross-view projection mechanism with complementary geometric supervisions, combining pointmap consistency with geometry foundation model-guided feature alignment. These designs enable controllable generation of temporally evolving multi-view observations with coherent appearance and geometrically consistent scene structures. Extensive experiments on 4D video generation dataset comprising simulated and real-world robotic manipulation scenarios demonstrate that GeoMVGen outperforms state-of-the-art methods in video quality, geometric accuracy, and cross-view consistency.
authors: Qiaoqiao Jia, Guile Wu, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting evolving 3D robot–object interactions consistently across viewpoints and under controllable actions and camera configurations.
Uses a video diffusion transformer with modality-specific adaptation modules for RGB appearance and pointmap geometry.
Connects modalities through cross-modal residuals and enforces cross-view correspondence with projection and geometric supervision.
Evaluations on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation scenarios report improved video quality, geometric accuracy, and cross-view consistency over existing methods.
