papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are the dominant architecture for video generation, but their quadratic attention complexity results in substantial computational cost and latency. Permuted block-sparse attention (PBSA) offers a promising approach to reducing this cost by selectively computing blocks of a semantically permuted attention matrix. However, existing approaches typically select only the top few key blocks for each query block, following a top-$p$ paradigm. We find that top-$p$ selection can be highly sample inefficient in high-entropy attention regimes, which are common in video generation. In these regimes, we show that sampling can provide substantially better approximations under the same computational budget. More generally, we cast block selection as importance sampling, where the top-scoring keys form an exact set that is computed in full and the remaining keys are represented by a sample drawn in proportion to their estimated attention and reweighted by inverse sampling probability. Building on this formulation, we present InstaGen, which can be parameterized by any PBSA method: it replaces the method's block selection with an exact set plus a weighted sample. Each query cluster draws one sample shared by all its queries, so the sampled keys form blocks amenable to efficient GPU execution. In this paper, we take the SVG family of PBSA methods and show that, on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen parameterized by SVG2 improves PSNR over SVG2 by 3.4 dB and 2 dB, respectively, at matched attention density, and by 1.6 dB and 2.2 dB at matched wall-clock time. On Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen also beats SVG-EAR by 1.1 dB PSNR at nearly the same density while running faster (1.65x against 1.48x over dense).
authors: Kislay Aditya Oj, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Sri Surya Varma Datla, Aditya Desai
bullets: Top-p block selection can be sample-inefficient when video attention has high entropy.
It treats block selection as importance sampling: exact computation for top-scoring keys and inverse-probability-weighted samples for the rest.
Each query cluster shares a sampled set, preserving block structure for efficient GPU execution.
With SVG2, InstaGen improves PSNR at matched attention density and wall-clock time on Wan2.1-T2V models.
It also outperforms SVG-EAR on Wan2.1-T2V-14B while running faster at nearly the same density.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of InstaGen. (a) Queries and keys are clustered into groups. (b) Centroid scores give each key group a probability π of being used by each query group. (c) The top key group is always kept; the remaining keys are sampled in proportion to π and weighted by 1/π. (d) Queries in a group share the same keys, so attention runs over dense blocks in one kernel.

Figure 4: InstaGen approximates attention more accurately than prior sparse methods. Left: relative L2 error of one self-attention call from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B against exact attention. Importance sampling gives the lowest error at every density, several times below SVG2. Right: per-block, per-head error over one full generation averaged across all steps. InstaGen (uniform, 16+16, no warm-up) keeps the error low everywhere at 32% density, while SVG2 (p=0.9, warm-up counted as zero error) leaves large errors in individual heads and layers despite computing 46%.

Figure 5: Warmup ablations on Wan2.1-T2V-14B (720p, 81 frames, 50 steps). InstaGen with uniform sampling runs its first 0, 5, 10 or 15 of 50 steps at full attention (warmup), ranging from 4+4% to 32+32% budget. SVG2 runs at its paper configurations at top-p 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9 and 0.99. A 5–10 step warmup matches or beats the 15 steps SVG2 uses. The hollow diamond is SVG2 without its one-layer warmup; the InstaGen runs have none. The prompt used is svg2 ex1, Appendix A.1.

Figure 6: InstaGen with importance sampling matches SVG2’s quality at much lower density. (a) PSNR against overall attention density (warm-up steps count as dense), averaged over 22 VBench prompts on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B (720p, 81 frames, 50 steps). SVG2 in its paper configuration (p=0.9) reaches 25.03 dB at 44.1%; InstaGen (importance sampling) reaches the same PSNR at 34.0% with the same 30% warm-up, and at 20.0% with no warm-up. (b) Denoising time against the number of frames on one H100 SXM, on one prompt (svg2 ex1, Appendix A.1; VAE decoding excluded), with InstaGen (importance sampling) at 4+4% with the 30% warm-up and at 14+14% with no warm-up, budgets at which it beats SVG2 (p=0.9) on PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS on this prompt at 81 frames. At 561 frames dense takes 162 min, SVG2 82.8 min (1.97×), and InstaGen 61.9 min (2.62×) with warm-up and 57.3 min (2.83×) without.

Figure 2: InstaGen gives higher quality than SVG2 at both matched density and matched latency on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B. Left: PSNR against generation time per video. Right: PSNR against attention density, the share of attention computed over the whole generation. SVG2 uses the configuration from its paper (Cq=100, Ck=500, full attention for the first 30% of steps, key floor 0.1) at top-p 0.5, 0.75, 0.9 and 0.95. InstaGen runs exact + sampled budgets from 4+4% to 32+32% at two clustering configurations for uniform and one for importance, with the same warmup and without it.

Table 1: Main results on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and 14B. PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS compare each video with the dense video from the same seed, and all quality metrics are averaged over the 22 VBench prompts. E+S: exact and sampled share of keys per sparse call with dense warmup, as prescribed by each baseline’s paper; InstaGen uses SVG2’s (first 30% of steps and 3% of layers). Density is overall, counting warmup calls as full attention. Speedup is end-to-end wall-clock on one H100 against a dense run. Bold: best sparse method in each column.
Table 2: The 22 VBench prompts.

papers.selection_reason: Improves diffusion-based video generation with sparse/block attention and importance sampling, fitting video diffusion and efficient attention.
papers.title: InstaGen: Group-Shared Importance Sampling for Fast Video Generation
papers.tldr: InstaGen accelerates video diffusion by replacing inefficient top-block selection with group-shared importance sampling, improving reconstruction quality at comparable compute.

papers.abstract: Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly. We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.
bullets: Targets DiTs’ inefficient uniform processing of mostly sparse visual content.
Routes tokens independently through MLP and self-attention operations, adapting compute by token, image, and denoising timestep.
Processes as few as 12.5% of tokens, substantially reducing training and inference costs.
Higher sparsity and model depth improve generation performance over unrouted baselines.
Token allocation is interpretable, correlating with visual content, noise level, and video motion.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models generate text by reversing a stochastic masking process. Unlike autoregressive LLMs, which generate text one token at a time, they can reveal many tokens in parallel, at the price of an error, since tokens revealed together are drawn independently. We show that this trade-off maps onto the statistical physics of driven many-particle systems. (i) For any data, the error of parallel generation is the entropy production of the generation process relative to the reversed masking process. (ii) For Markov data, generation is a random sequential adsorption process with labelled gaps, which we solve exactly for any number of steps. (iii) For many steps, the error becomes the dissipation of a slowly driven system: the unmasking schedule plays the role of the driving protocol, the number of steps that of its duration, and the error is set by a thermodynamic metric that we obtain in closed form from the mutual information between tokens. Optimal schedules are geodesics of this metric. The exact solution shows how correlations in the text shape both the error and the quality of the output. The longer the correlations, the more the error concentrates at the start of generation. Schedules that start with small steps then gain more, both in path error and in perplexity, and need fewer steps to reach their asymptotic behaviour.
bullets: Parallel decoding introduces error because tokens revealed together are sampled independently.
For arbitrary data, this error equals the entropy production relative to the reversed masking process.
For Markov data, generation maps to random sequential adsorption with labelled gaps and is solved exactly for any number of steps.
In the many-step regime, error is governed by a thermodynamic metric derived from token mutual information; optimal unmasking schedules follow its geodesics.
Longer-range correlations concentrate error early, favoring schedules with initially smaller steps that improve path error and perplexity with fewer steps.

papers.tldr: An exactly solvable statistical-physics framework explains and optimizes the accuracy–parallelism trade-off in masked diffusion text generation.

papers.abstract: Capturing scenes with extreme motion and high dynamic range is fundamentally constrained by trade-offs among temporal resolution, spatial detail, signal-to-noise ratio, and dynamic range under practical bandwidth, power, and quantum-efficiency limits. Conventional frame-based cameras therefore suffer from temporal undersampling, exposure-induced motion blur, and sensor saturation. The Complementary Vision Sensor (CVS) addresses these limitations by decomposing visual information across two complementary pathways, a spatially dense, temporally sparse, long-exposure RGB pathway and a temporally dense, spatially sparse, short-exposure patiotemporal difference pathway. Their complementary measurements provide appearance, structural, and motion cues across a wide dynamic range that enable reconstruction beyond conventional imaging. We present CoGenRec, a complementarity-driven generative reconstruction framework that unifies video deblurring, high-temporal-resolution frame interpolation, and HDR fusion. CoGenRec encodes complementary measurements into multi-scale spatiotemporal features using exposure-aware appearance modeling and bidirectional temporal propagation. These features constrain a video diffusion model and are injected into the VAE decoder to recover fine structures lost during latent-space compression, combining the scene fidelity of physical measurements with the appearance recovery capabilities of learned video priors. On SportsSloMo-CVS, CoGenRec improves PSNR over the strongest general-purpose baseline by 4.40 dB for deblurring, 3.89 dB for frame interpolation, and 5.04 dB for HDR fusion, respectively. It also achieves strong perceptual quality on 129 unseen scenes captured with real CVS. These results establish a unified approach to advance high-quality reconstruction under challenging motion and illumination conditions. Project page: https://cogenrec.github.io/.
bullets: Targets temporal undersampling, motion blur, and saturation caused by conventional frame-based cameras.
Encodes complementary spatially dense RGB and temporally dense difference measurements with exposure-aware modeling and bidirectional temporal propagation.
Conditions a video diffusion model and injects features into the VAE decoder to preserve fine details lost during latent compression.
Unifies video deblurring, frame interpolation, and HDR fusion in one reconstruction framework.
Reports PSNR gains over a general-purpose baseline on SportsSloMo-CVS and strong perceptual quality on 129 unseen real CVS scenes.

papers.abstract: One-step generators built on MeanFlow synthesize a video in a single function evaluation, yet inherit a rigid treatment of classifier-free guidance (CFG): the guidance scale is frozen during training or, at best, exposed as a single scalar. This conflicts with mounting evidence that the optimal guidance is not a constant but a field that varies with the noise level, with spatial content, and, for video, with frame position. Every existing remedy presupposes a multi-step sampler along which guidance can be re-scheduled--an assumption one-step models violate by construction. We resolve this tension through a single observation: because the MeanFlow target is an integral over a noise interval, an arbitrary guidance field can be absorbed into the target itself and compiled into one evaluation. We formalize this as the interval-integrated CFG identity, prove that the compiled guidance carries no schedule-discretization error and can thus match or exceed any finite multi-step sampler, and instantiate it as AGAVE, which equips the average-velocity field with a learnable temporal schedule, a free motion-saliency spatial modulation, and a frame-position asymmetry. Adding fewer than ten scalars at zero inference cost, AGAVE surpasses all one-step baselines on VBench, UCF-101 and MSR-VTT while matching multi-step guided sampling. Project repository: https://github.com/YMlinfeng/AGAVE.
bullets: One-step MeanFlow generators traditionally use a fixed or scalar CFG scale, despite guidance varying across noise levels, spatial content, and video frames.
The proposed interval-integrated CFG identity absorbs an arbitrary guidance field into the MeanFlow target.
AGAVE adds a learnable temporal schedule, spatial motion-saliency modulation, and frame-position asymmetry.
It uses fewer than ten additional scalars with no inference-time cost.
The method surpasses one-step baselines on VBench, UCF-101, and MSR-VTT, while matching multi-step guided sampling.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of AGAVE. A single MeanFlow DiT uθ emits a conditional/unconditional velocity pair whose guidance gap ∆v is modulated along three axes – a learnable Beta schedule over noise level τ , a free motion-saliency map M over space, and a learnable frame-position profile ρ(f) – forming a continuous guidance field ω(zτ , τ, f). The interval-integrated CFG operator (Thm. 1) absorbs this field into the average-velocity target, compiling a full time-, space- and frame-varying schedule into one evaluation. The schedule parameters ϕ are learned by distilling a multi-step adaptively guided teacher; inference remains strictly 1-NFE.

Figure 9. Qualitative comparison. Rows are methods, columns are boundary and interior frames of one clip, with magnified insets. AGAVE removes the saturated highlights of scalar guidance on static regions and sharpens fast-moving foreground, while keeping more diverse boundary frames. More results are in Appendix E.

papers.title: Guidance Is a Field, Not a Scalar: Interval-Integrated Classifier-Free Guidance for One-Step Video Generation
papers.tldr: AGAVE compiles noise-, spatial-, and frame-dependent classifier-free guidance into a single MeanFlow evaluation for stronger one-step video generation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become an effective approach for improving video generation, but its success depends heavily on reliable reward models. Existing methods either map videos directly to opaque scalar scores or generate free-form rationales that are not explicitly optimized as the basis of the final judgment. We propose ArtiVidRM, a verifiable, artifact-as-rubrics video reward model that follows an observe-then-score paradigm. It first identifies visible generation artifacts and organizes them into a structured artifact list, then uses these artifacts as explicit rubrics for quality assessment. This intermediate representation grounds each score in concrete video-level evidence, making the reward more interpretable and informative for optimization. We further introduce a multi-reward reinforcement learning strategy to jointly optimize artifact prediction and quality assessment. The reward decomposes into complementary objectives that evaluate artifact prediction quality, including semantic coverage and prediction efficiency, together with a pairwise preference objective that supervises quality ranking through score differences. By jointly optimizing the intermediate artifact representation and the downstream preference prediction, the model learns to produce informative artifact lists while improving the accuracy of video quality assessment. Experiments show that ArtiVidRM achieves state-of-the-art performance on video preference benchmarks, provides effective signals for video diffusion optimization, and enables artifact-guided refinement of closed-source video generators.
bullets: Addresses opaque scalar rewards and ungrounded free-form rationales in video-generation reinforcement learning.
Uses an observe-then-score pipeline: predict a structured list of visible artifacts, then assess quality based on those artifacts.
Jointly optimizes artifact prediction and pairwise quality ranking through multiple reward objectives, including semantic coverage and prediction efficiency.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on video preference benchmarks and useful signals for video diffusion optimization.
Supports artifact-guided refinement of closed-source video generators.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models for video generation have achieved remarkable success, yet precise motion control under explicit user guidance remains challenging. Recent noise-warping methods introduce temporal correlations by warping the noise according to the user-provided motion signal. However, standard spatial warping generally disrupts the noise's i.i.d. Gaussian structure, requiring distribution correction, such as Jacobian-based correction, but at a substantial computational overhead. We propose Householder Motion Embedding (HME), which encodes the motion signal into the noise through a sequence of Householder reflections that together form an orthogonal transformation applied to each location's channel vector. HME exactly preserves the spatial Gaussian structure within each frame while introducing cross-frame correlations that promote temporally consistent video. HME is agnostic to the network architecture and integrates directly into standard video diffusion fine-tuning pipelines. Experiments on different scenarios show that HME matches or outperforms the state of the art, while achieving a 2.7x speedup over noise warping. These results demonstrate that channel-space Householder transformations offer a principled and efficient alternative to noise warping for motion-controllable video generation.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of precise motion control in video diffusion models.
Uses a sequence of Householder reflections as an orthogonal channel-space transformation guided by user motion.
Preserves each frame’s spatial i.i.d. Gaussian noise structure while creating cross-frame temporal correlations.
Architecture-agnostic and directly compatible with standard video diffusion fine-tuning pipelines.
Reportedly matches or outperforms prior methods across scenarios and runs 2.7× faster than noise warping.

papers.abstract: Flow matching (FM) generators often face a quality-coverage tradeoff. Inference-time techniques such as classifier-free guidance raise quality, but at the cost of coverage. We revisit a basic property of FM -- an intermediate noisy image corresponds to multiple valid targets, which is collapsed into a single mean velocity by design. This can cover multiple modes of the distribution under ideal conditions, but is it optimal in practice? We instead investigate if directly modeling the modes of intermediate states better covers the modes of the full distribution. To do so, we augment the predictor with a randomly drawn low-dimensional code $z$, sampling $K$ candidate velocities for each training sample. We then apply the loss only to the best-matching candidate. This winner-take-all objective enables different codes to specialize and collectively cover different modes. Furthermore, this term naturally enables a new form of guidance, auxiliary conditioning scaling, which complements traditional guidance methods. Together, these two guidance mechanisms show that our method substantially improves the quality--coverage frontier. We validate on ImageNet-256, using two different testbeds, SiT and RAEv2. Given less than 3% of the original SiT pretraining compute for post-training, at the 67% Recall point, our method reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 19.22 to 5.91. On RAEv2, at the 70% Recall point, it reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 16.83 to 3.18.
bullets: Flow matching can collapse multiple valid targets for a noisy intermediate image into a single mean velocity, limiting coverage.
The method adds a random low-dimensional code to predict multiple candidate velocities and uses a winner-take-all loss so candidates specialize in different modes.
This enables auxiliary conditioning scaling, a new guidance mechanism that complements classifier-free guidance.
On ImageNet-256, the method substantially improves quality–coverage metrics on both SiT and RAEv2 testbeds, with less than 3% of SiT pretraining compute for post-training.

papers.abstract: Masked discrete diffusion models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive generation, but iterative sampling can be costly, and intractable sequence likelihoods complicate reward fine-tuning. We introduce IDRF, a framework for reward fine-tuning of few-step masked discrete diffusion generators. Starting from a standard reverse-KL-regularized objective, IDRF replaces the intractable sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization. With an optimal auxiliary denoiser, we prove that the population inverse-distillation loss upper-bounds the sequence-level KL divergence to the reference distribution. IDRF optimizes a trajectory-based surrogate of this loss without reference-model rollouts, so the student keeps its own few-step sampler. We view few-step generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and optimize reward with a clipped policy-gradient objective over the student's trajectories. Across DNA, image, and text generation, IDRF achieves high reward with up to $32\times$ fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.
bullets: Targets expensive iterative sampling and intractable sequence-level KL regularization in masked discrete diffusion.
Replaces the sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization and proves an upper bound under an optimal auxiliary denoiser.
Optimizes a trajectory-based, clipped policy-gradient objective over the student’s own few-step sampler.
Across DNA, image, and text generation, achieves high reward with up to 32× fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation offers efficient generation with diffusion and flow models, but preserving quality with only a few sampling steps remains challenging. Distribution-matching methods via score distillation provide a strong foundation, yet they rely on accurately tracking the student's changing distribution. At intermediate generation steps in few-step sampling, student-score estimation can be difficult, and commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Flow matching allows a more flexible approach to supervision through velocity fields constructed from the student's sampling process. Building on this perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), which uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields and turn their disagreement into feedback for learning. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives. We further develop VA-TDM, which follows trajectory distribution matching: providing supervision for partial denoising along the student trajectory. Beyond this, VA-TDM combines transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions. Extensive results show that VA-TDM is powerful for learning few-step generators, achieving state-of-the-art four-step performance in both text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scaling effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3. In particular, our VA-TDM-H3 notably outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the original many-step H3 according to human preference.
authors: Yihong Luo, Tianyu Pang, Tianyang Hu

Uses trajectory distribution matching with online transition-aware velocity learning and dual-form supervision.
Achieves state-of-the-art four-step text-to-image and text-to-video results, including scaling to the 33B MiniMax-H3 model.

papers.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

papers.abstract: For decades, diagnostic pathology has relied on thin two-dimensional (2D) tissue sections, despite biological tissues exhibiting inherently three-dimensional (3D) morphological organization. Because a single section captures only one focal plane, important morphological cues along the z-axis are inevitably discarded, limiting tissue representation for both human interpretation and computational analysis. In this work, we propose a generative framework that learns z-axis morphological priors from pathology z-stack data, offering a cost-effective alternative to dedicated volumetric imaging, and transfers this knowledge to conventional single-plane histopathology. Specifically, an image-to-video (I2V) latent diffusion model (LDM) is trained to synthesize a pseudo z-stack from a single 2D image, capturing plausible morphological variations across adjacent focal planes rather than reconstructing physical tissue volumes. To enable deployment on large-scale clinical datasets without native z-stack acquisition, we further introduce a prior-preserving mixture fine-tuning strategy that adapts the model to new domains while retaining the learned z-axis morphological prior. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the synthesized pseudo z-stacks exhibit realistic cross-plane morphological continuity and consistently improve downstream prostate cancer classification compared with conventional 2D representations. Our results suggest that learning transferable z-axis priors from limited z-stack data provides a practical way to enrich routine pathology images with complementary morphological information. papers.abstract: Diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by denoising multiple draft tokens in parallel. Their training uses anchor sampling to construct compact draft queries and performs cross-attention with a block-sparse mask over a much longer context. We empirically show that acceptance length remains stable as context scales with a fixed query budget, while increasing the query budget yields diminishing quality gains, jointly establishing a practical regime with queries far shorter than the context. No existing context parallelism (CP) method jointly exploits this query--context asymmetry and meets the nonlinear, sample-dependent load-balancing requirement created by anchor sampling. We present Split-KV, an exact CP method that keeps key/value shards local and limits per-layer attention communication to query-sized tensors, making this communication independent of context length. Its global query view further enables a cost-aware longest-processing-time-first (LPT) strategy that balances context key/value chunks by their realized attention cost. At a CP size of 64, Split-KV retains 85--91\% weak-scaling efficiency and achieves up to $3.67\times$ speedup over the fastest available CP baseline. LPT achieves $<$1\% imbalance and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best load-balancing baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/zxgx/verl.
authors: Geng Zhang, Fangzhao Zhang, Cong Xie, Tiantian Fan, Yang You
bullets: Diffusion drafters use compact draft queries to attend over much longer, block-sparse contexts.

A global query view enables longest-processing-time-first scheduling to balance sample-dependent attention costs.
At context-parallel size 64, Split-KV achieves 85–91% weak-scaling efficiency and up to 3.67× speedup over the fastest baseline.
LPT reduces load imbalance to below 1% and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best compared balancer.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention accelerates few-step video diffusion transformers by computing a few key blocks exactly and compensating for the rest. However, existing sparse attention still faces key challenges, including identification overhead from finding critical blocks at every denoising step, suboptimal budget allocation that sets sparsity budgets uniformly or by local metrics, and cross-step error accumulation as reused masks or clusters go stale. Observing that the errors left on skipped blocks cancel each other once every key is compensated, we propose DecoupAttn, a new paradigm of decoupled sparse attention: semantic clusters compensate every key, and exact attention corrects their error on a few blocks fixed once offline by position. To support this paradigm, we introduce Distortion Budget, a rate-distortion objective for budget allocation that places exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads where it removes the most distortion that compensation leaves in the final latent. Built on this budget, we further propose Reassign Cache, in which each step reassigns the drifting keys to cached centroids and refreshes compensation while the budgeted blocks stay fixed. Moreover, DecoupAttn is training-free: a few calibration clips compile one plan offline, and inference runs standard block-sparse kernels with one fused compensation kernel. Our code will be released after submission.
authors: Yanjin Li, Bingbing Qiu, Qiang Huang, Rui Qian, Yanfeng Li, Jian Wang, Xiaoying Tang, Mingda Zhang
bullets: Targets identification overhead, poor uniform/local budget allocation, and stale masks or clusters in sparse video diffusion attention.

Introduces Distortion Budget to allocate exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads based on its effect on final-latent distortion.
Uses Reassign Cache to update drifting key-to-centroid assignments and refresh compensation at each denoising step.
Compiles the plan from a few calibration clips and performs inference with block-sparse kernels plus one fused compensation kernel; no training is required.

papers.abstract: Digital human e-commerce video generation requires preserving product appearance, human identity, and overall video style during dynamic demonstrations. Although recent models support multiple reference images, their general conditioning schemes do not explicitly distinguish the asymmetric roles of "what is presented" and "who presents it." Consequently, generated videos may favor a single reference, resulting in product distortion, identity drift, or single-reference collapse. To address this issue, we propose DualCast, a role-addressed dual-image conditioning framework for video generation. By explicitly modeling the distinct roles of product and human conditions, DualCast reduces role ambiguity and feature competition between references. First, a dual-spatiotemporal slot injection mechanism VAE-encodes the product and human images separately and places their latent features at the front and rear boundaries of the DiT sequence, enabling sequence-level condition separation and directed injection. Second, a mask-guided region-weighted loss strengthens supervision over product, face, and product-face overlap regions, improving generation fidelity in critical areas. Third, image condition dropout enables a single model to support dual-image, product-only, and human-only generation. In addition, we construct a curated dataset of 10K e-commerce videos for model training. Experimental results demonstrate the strong performance of DualCast.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yibo Zhao, Senlin Cheng, Bolei Xu, Xiaobo Li, Can Ye, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses product distortion, identity drift, and single-reference collapse caused by ambiguous multi-image conditioning.

Uses image-condition dropout to support dual-image, product-only, and human-only generation.
Trained on a curated dataset of 10K e-commerce videos; the abstract reports strong experimental performance without specific metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DualCast. The product and presenter images are independently VAE-encoded and placed at the front and rear boundaries of the extended latent sequence, respectively. Only intermediate video latents are denoised, supervised, and decoded. Both reference CLIP embeddings combine with the text prompt as cross-attention context. Product and face masks define region-weighted supervision, while condition dropout enables dual-image, product-only, and human-only inference.

Figure 4. Qualitative Comparison Results. Compared with existing methods, our approach demonstrates advantages in three aspects: (1) Facial Feature Consistency — Our method preserves the source person’s facial identity during video generation, avoiding identity drift or distortion; (2) Product Consistency — Product details from the reference image, including appearance, texture, and logos, are accurately reproduced, maintaining high visual fidelity; (3) Style Decoupling Capability — The overall style of the generated video is not irreversibly influenced by the reference image, achieving flexible decoupling between content transfer and style control, making the generation results more suitable for e-commerce live streaming scenarios.

Figure 1. A single fine-tuned DualCast model unifies three inference modes. A (Dual-image): Using dual-spatiotemporal slot injection, the model assigns roles to and preserves both product appearance and presenter identity. B (Product-only): When the human condition is omitted, the model generates high-quality presenter-led promotional videos based on the product. C (Human-only): When the product condition is omitted, the model generates high-quality presenter-led promotional videos based on the person.

Product and presenter assets are collected or synthesized, quality-filtered, and paired to generate e-commerce-oriented prompts and initial frames. Candidate videos are subsequently filtered according to visual quality, temporal consistency, and prompt compliance. Product and face masks are precomputed for regionweighted training. papers.abstract: Diffusion image generators are successful due to accurate denoising networks and strong numerical samplers. Yet the two components are not fully matched. During sampling, the denoiser predicts for the next step based on flawed input that differ much from the real data. This train-test gap, or exposure bias, caps image generation quality (i.e., blurry, lacking in details or awkward in shape). To mitigate the problem, we propose PEEK, a novel training-free deterministic sampler plugin. At each eligible denoising step, PEEK first performs a provisional one-step update, evaluates the denoiser once at the look-ahead state, and interpolates it with the one-step-later prediction to form the next noisy state. By taking the additional step, we obtain a generally more-image-like prediction from the higher-signal noisy state, mitigating the exposure bias. To optimize the interpolation positions, PEEK searches for an interpolation schedule search made efficient by the prefix and baseline noise-schedule-rebasing caches. On 8 pixel-space and latent-space diffusion models with unconditional, label-guided, and text-guided settings across various output resolutions, PEEK consistently improves over NFE-matched baselines, with FID improvements up to 49.3\% at minimal extra computation cost (e.g., the one-time-per-model calibration takes at most 2.2 minutes across our experiments.). Project website is at https://dachengruoque.github.io/PEEK-Video/.

papers.abstract: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

papers.abstract: Video character replacement aims to replace actors while preserving facial expressions, motions, and scene dynamics. Existing methods typically rely on masked generation with pose guidance, limiting fine-grained expression and motion preservation in complex scenes. We propose ReXMo, an end-to-end framework that supports single-, multi-, and selective character replacement scenarios. ReXMo introduces paired triplet supervision, where synthesized driving videos and original videos share identical performances but different identities, enabling scalable training through synthetic data generation. An In-Context Diffusion Transformer learns identity transformation by jointly conditioning on driving videos, reference identities, and text prompts, while an Expression Enhancement Adapter improves facial expression preservation in multi-person scenes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReXMo outperforms existing methods in identity fidelity, motion consistency, expression preservation, and visual quality. Our dataset and code will be publicly released.
bullets: Addresses limitations of masked generation and pose guidance in preserving fine-grained expressions and motion in complex scenes.
Uses paired triplet supervision from synthetic driving/original video pairs with matching performances but different identities.
Employs an In-Context Diffusion Transformer conditioned on driving videos, reference identities, and text prompts for identity transformation.
Adds an Expression Enhancement Adapter to improve facial expression preservation in multi-person scenes.
Experiments report improved identity fidelity, motion consistency, expression preservation, and visual quality over existing methods; code and data are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Diffusion distillation is widely adopted to accelerate sampling, and the resulting few-step models are broadly believed to match or even surpass their multi-step teachers in generation. However, standard evaluations such as GenEval2 typically draw only one sample per prompt, so improved scores may fail to reveal losses in distribution coverage. We therefore revisit whether distilled models truly match their teachers beyond single-draw performance using \textbf{pass@$\mathbf{k}$}, which measures the probability that at least one of $k$ independent samples satisfies a quality criterion. At $k{=}1$, pass@$k$ reduces to standard single-draw evaluation. As $k$ grows, the curve reveals whether additional draws find genuinely different successes or merely revisit the same modes, directly exposing how broadly a model covers the space of valid outputs. We first show that classifier-free guidance (CFG), whose quality--coverage tradeoff is well established, is the clearest case: higher guidance improves pass@$1$, but its advantage shrinks and reverses at larger $k$. Applying pass@$k$ to few-step distilled models, we find the same tradeoff splits along training objectives: distribution-matching objectives concentrate the student's output distribution, boosting early-hit rates while eroding large-budget coverage, whereas consistency and trajectory-based objectives better preserve the teacher's coverage even at large $k$. We further show that this tradeoff extends to few-step causal video generation. Our findings reveal a previously overlooked cost of diffusion distillation: across both image and video generation, the choice of training objective fundamentally determines whether a few-step model inherits its teacher's distribution coverage or trades it away for single-draw quality.
bullets: Single-draw metrics may hide distribution-coverage losses because they use only one sample per prompt.
Pass@$k$ measures whether any of $k$ samples meets a quality criterion, exposing how coverage changes with more sampling attempts.
Higher classifier-free guidance improves pass@1 but can reduce performance at larger $k$, indicating narrower coverage.
Distribution-matching distillation favors early successes but concentrates outputs, while consistency and trajectory-based objectives better preserve teacher coverage.
The same quality–coverage tradeoff appears in few-step image and causal video generation.

papers.abstract: High frame rate HDR video is important in applications such as autonomous driving and scientific imaging, where rapid motion and extreme illumination often occur simultaneously. Conventional frame cameras face a trade-off between temporal resolution and dynamic range, while event cameras provide complementary high-speed brightness-change measurements over a wide illumination range. These properties have motivated event-based HDR reconstruction, with existing methods broadly following event-only and hybrid event-frame paradigms. Event-only HDR reconstruction, however, suffers from brightness and color drift due to the lack of absolute intensity references. Hybrid event-frame methods alleviate this ambiguity using low-dynamic-range (LDR) frames as anchors, but most perform one-to-one HDR reconstruction at available LDR timestamps. In this work, we investigate single-reference HDR temporal expansion, reconstructing N HDR frames from one LDR reference and events instead of N aligned LDR observations. We develop HIVE-Diff, an event-conditioned video diffusion framework that decomposes the task into event-guided temporal generation and HDR content completion. Because paired real HDR-event data are scarce, we train on synthetic data and adapt the model to real event domains using LDR-event sequences as proxy supervision with teacher-student distillation. Experiments on synthetic and multiple real-world datasets demonstrate strong reconstruction quality and robust real-data adaptation.
bullets: Addresses the need for simultaneous high temporal resolution and wide dynamic range in fast, high-contrast scenes.
Generates N HDR frames from one LDR reference and events, avoiding the need for aligned LDR frames at every timestamp.
Uses event-guided temporal generation followed by HDR content completion in a video diffusion framework.
Trains on synthetic data and adapts to real event domains through teacher-student distillation with LDR-event proxy supervision.
Reports strong reconstruction quality and robust real-data adaptation across synthetic and multiple real-world datasets.

papers.abstract: Video dubbing aims to synthesize lip movements that match target speech while preserving the speaker identity, head pose, and background of a source video. Existing editors are predominantly trained via self-reconstruction under original paired audio, even though the source mouth becomes a conflicting target when driving speech is replaced. We introduce \emph{replacement-aware cross-audio supervision}: paired-audio samples use full-frame reconstruction, whereas unpaired replacement-audio samples mask out source-mouth reconstruction losses and supervise the mouth solely through audio--visual synchronization while preserving unmasked facial regions and background. Because offline dubbing provides the complete source video and target speech beforehand, we present \method, a full-context diffusion editor that uses matched trajectory regression to transfer CFG-guided teacher trajectories to a two-step student and distribution matching to recover visual quality after compression. We will release the curated training dataset, VidDub-Bench, fixed paired- and cross-audio evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code. Across three training seeds, masking out conflicting source-mouth reconstruction improves cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833. At two NFE, the final student provides the strongest cross-audio synchronization and visual-speech recognition among the evaluated methods, with competitive visual fidelity and source preservation.
bullets: Existing self-reconstruction training conflicts with replaced target speech because the source mouth is an incorrect target.
Replacement-aware cross-audio supervision masks source-mouth losses for unpaired replacement audio while preserving other facial regions and the background.
A full-context diffusion editor uses matched trajectory regression and distribution matching to produce a two-step student.

Masking improves cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833 across three training seeds; the two-step student achieves the strongest reported cross-audio synchronization and visual-speech recognition, with competitive fidelity and source preservation.
The authors will release VidDub-Bench, evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code.

papers.abstract: Low-quality facial videos suffer from missing fine details, while AI-generated videos may additionally contain implausible teeth and lip movements that do not match the speech. Restoring the mouth region is particularly challenging: enhancing existing details can preserve structural errors, whereas regenerating them risks changing facial identity and articulation. We propose an audio-guided facial video restoration framework that reconstructs unreliable mouth details and aligns lip movements with the speech while preserving facial identity and temporal consistency. Built on a video diffusion transformer, our framework mixes input video latents with noise to retain useful source information while allowing corrupted details to be regenerated. Audio guides lip movements, reference images constrain facial appearance, and previously generated frames promote temporal consistency. We train the model in two stages, first learning visual restoration from degraded images and videos, then learning audio-guided lip correction from degraded dubbed videos. The resulting model supports both restoration with the original audio and visual dubbing with replacement audio. On talking-head restoration benchmarks, our method achieves the lowest LPIPS and DISTS and the best lip synchronization scores among the evaluated restoration baselines. Qualitative results on AI-generated videos further show improvements in facial detail and mouth-region appearance, including clearer tooth boundaries and lip contours.
bullets: Addresses low-quality or AI-generated talking-head videos with missing facial detail and speech-inconsistent teeth or lip movements.
Uses a video diffusion transformer that mixes video latents with noise, combining source information with controlled detail regeneration.
Audio guides lip motion; reference images preserve facial appearance; prior frames support temporal consistency.
Trains in two stages for visual restoration and audio-guided lip correction, supporting original-audio restoration and visual dubbing.
Achieves the best reported LPIPS, DISTS, and lip-synchronization scores among evaluated restoration baselines, with qualitative gains in tooth boundaries and lip contours.

papers.abstract: Pose-driven human video diffusion animates a person from a single reference image and a target pose sequence, yet it struggles to preserve identity, rendering the face and garments unfaithfully as the pose departs from it. Personalization is the standard remedy, but its supervision is missing: one image fixes identity at a single pose, while a multi-pose subject video cannot be assumed in practice. Instead, we synthesize the missing supervision. A domain-tuned, pose-conditioned generator produces pseudo-ground-truth frames at selected key poses. An inference-time reference-only sampler steers these candidates toward the subject and keeps the most identity-consistent. A per-subject low-rank adapter then trains on static clips of them, configured from the reference alone, with no subject video, ground truth, or labels. Although lower in fidelity, these synthetic frames supervise more effectively than real ones. Real frames as captured carry motion that erodes the temporal prior, while a static clip conveys appearance alone. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves the base on every metric, inverts the identity-versus-motion trade-off, and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real frames despite using none. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/SadmanPinon/one-image-is-enough.
bullets: Addresses identity drift in faces and garments when the target pose differs substantially from a single reference image.
Generates pseudo-ground-truth frames at key poses, filters them with a reference-only sampler, and trains a per-subject low-rank adapter on static clips.
Requires only one reference image—no subject video, ground-truth frames, or labels.
On TikTok and UBC Fashion, improves the base model on every reported metric and matches or surpasses adaptation using five real frames.
Synthetic static clips can supervise more effectively than real motion videos because they preserve appearance without disrupting temporal priors.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. From one reference image xref and a driving pose sequence P , a pose-conditioned generator G synthesizes pose-targeted pseudo-ground-truth frames Dpseudo of the subject. (a) Reward-guided generation: for each key pose, G draws several candidates as an interacting particle system and resamples them in-loop toward a DINO body-similarity reward to xref , then selects the final frame by ArcFace face identity. Every reward is read from the reference alone (our reference-only reward-guided sampler). (b) Test-time personalization: a per-subject LoRA ∆θ adapts the frozen base animator Fθ on static clips of the selected frames. The adapted model Fθ+∆θ renders the personalized video V̂ . No subject video, no ground truth, and no human feedback are used.

Figure 3. Temporal stability. Top: the driving frames. For Base (middle) and Ours (bottom), the leftmost column is that method’s output frame and the remaining columns are consecutive framedifference maps over the same frames. The non-personalized base produces widespread inter-frame residual across the face and torso (temporal flicker), whereas our adapted model confines residual to true motion boundaries and stays stable, reducing mean interframe residual by 60% over the frames shown. Brighter indicates larger frame-to-frame change.

Figure 7. Human preference study. Distribution of 1–5 ratings for ours, Animate-X, the unadapted base, and Moore-AnimateAnyone, on four axes. Thirty-four respondents, 180 ratings per bar group. Ours places 93% of appearance-alignment ratings at 4–5, against 38% for the base model; the ordering is the same on all four axes. Protocol in Appendix B.2.

Figure 8. In-Domain Comparisons: Diverse Motions and Backgrounds. Examples illustrating variations in background, motion complexity, and clothing style. Our approach consistently preserves holistic appearance and pose alignment while producing sharper, more realistic details than competing methods.

Figure 9. In-Domain Comparisons: Diverse Appearance and Illumination. Examples covering variations in skin tone, lighting conditions, and clothing texture. Our approach maintains consistent subject appearance and realistic fine-grained details across all scenarios, clearly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Figure 6. Pose-conditioned generator G. G is built on FLUX.1 Kontext [21] paired with a pose ControlNet [57]. The target pose is VAE-encoded and read by a frozen ControlNet (14 joint blocks, 38 unified blocks), whose pose-aware features condition the main DiT. The reference image and initial noise are encoded and denoised by the main DiT, into which we inject the trainable LoRA [13]; a text encoder supplies the prompt. The output latent is VAE-decoded to the subject rendered under the target pose. Backbone weights are frozen (snowflake); only the LoRA adapters are trained (flame).

Figure 5. Pseudo-frame count and supervision source. (a) FVD (orange) is lowest at K=5; FaceID (teal) dips at K=9 and peaks at K=21 at a similar FVD (values from Tab. 6). (b) Seven-metric comparison of supervision sources (outward = better, per-axis min–max over the rows of Tab. 5): Ours forms nearly the outer envelope, while self-distillation collapses on body similarity and temporal consistency.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on hard poses. For two subjects we show the reference and driving pose alongside the base, our adapted model, and ground truth. Insets crop the face. The base reconstructs identity and garment detail inconsistently as the pose departs from the reference, while our adaptation preserves both.

Figure 10. Cross-Domain Comparisons: Animated Characters. Examples from the Unseen100-Val evaluation set featuring 2D and 3D animated characters unseen during training. Our approach generalizes beyond photorealistic subjects, faithfully preserving stylized appearance details and character proportions while maintaining temporal coherence under complex motion.

Figure 11. Adaptation is bounded by pseudo-frame quality. Top (HQ): high-quality pseudo frames (Supervision) yield faithful adapted outputs (Output frames). Bottom (LQ): degraded pseudo frames for the same subject yield weaker outputs. This is why the reference-only sampler selects high-quality frames before adaptation.

Table 12. Sensitivity to the generator’s domain tuning. G’s LoRA receives from no tuning (off-the-shelf FLUX.1 Kontext with the pose ControlNet) to our default of 4,000 steps, with the rest of the pipeline fixed. Teacher is the fidelity of the selected pseudo-frame to the real frame at that pose, and downstream is the adapted model’s video quality (trim, 3 TikTok sequences).

Table 2. Quantitative comparison on cross-domain performance on the Unseen100-Val set after training on TikTok. Off the training distribution, our adaptation reaches the only FVD below 100 (92.5) and the lowest dtSSD, while every other method stays above 125.

Peak GPU is the maximum resident device memory during the stage, and Alloc. the torch allocator peak where the pipeline reports it (protocol in Appendix F.1).

The one-time peak is the maximum over the two stages, not their sum. Of it, 43.6 GiB is the frozen base and 9.2 GiB our update (Tab. 18). Inference costs what the base costs, as the merged adapter adds no parameters. Protocol in App. F.
Table 7. Reward-design ablation (on a tuning subset). The two reference-only rewards assigned to in-loop steering versus final selection. Steering with DINO and selecting with ArcFace is best.

Table 6. Number of pseudo frames K. We sweep the number of self-generated supervision frames used for per-subject adaptation. FaceID and BodySIM are over the full video; K=5 is the best balanced configuration.

Table 11. Per-subject LoRA rank r (on a tuning subset). Adaptation quality as the rank of the per-subject update varies. Quality improves with capacity up to r=128, our default; beyond it (r=256) the adapter over-fits the few pseudo-frames and quality regresses, marking a clear optimum. Absolute scores differ from the main tables because this sweep runs on a tuning subset.

Table 5. Supervision source. All rows share the adaptation recipe; only the supervision source changes. FaceID and BodySIM are over the full video, on the TikTok dataset. The standalone quality of G appears in Tab. 4.

Table 3. Cross-reenactment (Unseen100-Val). Each subject is driven by a different subject’s motion, so no aligned ground truth exists; we measure identity against the reference (FaceID, BodySIM) and pose obedience against the driving sequence (PoseAcc). Adaptation raises appearance fidelity while leaving pose obedience essentially unchanged, as the pose-conditioning pathway is frozen.

Table 18. Composition of the adaptation memory peak. Resident sizes follow from each checkpoint’s parameter count and load precision: bf16 for the frozen modules, and fp32 with gradients and two AdamW moments for the low-rank update. The final line is the measured peak minus the resident modules above it.

Table 10. Quality versus fine-tuning time. Per-subject adaptation quality at different numbers of fine-tuning steps and the time they take on a single H100 (K=5, TikTok). Quality saturates within the first five steps, our default. Longer budgets improve only identity, and not monotonically.

Table 14. Resampling schedule. Selected pseudo-ground-truth frame fidelity to the real frame as a function of the denoising window over which particles are resampled and the churn strength η that re-noises duplicated particles (N=8; mean over the K supervised poses × 3 sequences). Pseudo-ground-truth frame quality is largely insensitive to the schedule; the back-half-with-churn default is used for its downstream stability.

Table 13. Particle count N . Selected pseudo-ground-truth frame fidelity to the real frame (mean over the K supervised poses × 3 sequences) and per-pseudo-frame generation time, as the number of reward-guided particles varies. Frame quality is largely saturated already by our default N=8, while sampling time grows roughly linearly, so larger populations cost compute without further gain. Time is the per-pseudo-frame sampling cost on a single H100.

Table 16. Composition of the Unseen100-Val dataset. Each attribute group independently covers all 100 videos; rows within a group sum to 100 (or to 80 for appearance and setting, which apply only to the real-human videos).

Table 9. Identity measured by recognizers not used by the pipeline. Pseudo-frames are selected with ArcFace, so identity is re-scored with FaceNet512 and SFace, which are not used in selection. Faces are detected once and every recognizer embeds the identical crop. A frame is scored only when a face is found in the ground truth and in both arms (33 pairs for base vs ours, 30 for the three-arm comparison, trim regime, 3 TikTok sequences). Ours-FN selects with FaceNet512 instead of ArcFace.

Table 15. Key-pose selection. How the K supervised poses are chosen from the driving sequence, at fixed K: farthest-point sampling in keypoint space (ours) vs. random and uniform-in-time selection, each adapted with an identical step budget and evaluated on the generated video (mean over 3 sequences). On this subset the three strategies are within noise of one another, indicating the gain comes from supervising diverse poses at all rather than from the specific selection rule.

Table 19. Amortization of the one-time cost. Adaptation (9.3 min) is paid once per reference image, and each subsequent video of that reference costs only inference. Since adapted and base inference are the same computation (Tab. 17), we use a single render time for both, the measured 7.46 min for a full-length 305-frame video, so the ratio reflects the one-time cost alone. Average cost per video is (9.3 + 7.46n)/n, which decays as 1/n and is within 5% of the unadapted base by n=25.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models (AR-VDMs) enable real-time, long-horizon video generation but degrade rapidly once the inference horizon outruns the training horizon, due to compounding exposure bias. To stabilize long rollouts, recent methods heuristically adopt frame sink, keeping initial frames as a persistent model context, inspired by attention sinks in LLMs. We revisit this design and find that the mechanism by which initial frames stabilize long-range consistency in AR-VDMs is not an LLM-style attention sink; instead, long-range consistency is anchored through a sparse subset of attention heads, while the majority of heads predominantly capture local temporal dynamics. This observation reveals an over-conditioning pathology in existing frame-sink strategies: by universally exposing every head to the pinned initial-frame context, the model becomes prone to collapsing motion toward the low-dynamic modes of the teacher during model distillation. We propose Disen-Forcing, a distillation-time plug-in for AR-VDMs that disentangles and reinforces this head specialization through disentangled context routing and motion-disentangling regularization. On long-horizon video generation benchmarks, Disen-Forcing simultaneously improves long-range consistency and motion dynamics of base AR-VDMs, a trade-off that sink-based methods fail to balance.
bullets: AR-VDMs suffer compounding exposure bias when generating beyond their training horizon.
Long-range consistency relies on a sparse subset of attention heads, not a universal LLM-style attention sink.
Conventional frame-sink strategies over-condition all heads and can collapse motion toward low-dynamic modes.
Disen-Forcing uses disentangled context routing and motion-disentangling regularization during distillation.
Experiments show improved long-range consistency and motion dynamics without the trade-off of sink-based methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Temporal attention patterns across models and heads. (a) Per-head attention to the initial and current frames across AR-VDMs, averaged over 50 MovieGenBench [32] prompts and denoising timesteps. Most heads attend predominantly to the current frame, while a sparse subset concentrates attention on the initial frame. (b) Attention distributions of representative Self-Forcing heads across seven rollout steps, at ODE initialization (left) and after DMD (right). Working Heads exhibit local temporal patterns, whereas Anchor Heads attend persistently to the initial frame.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison and ablation. Self-Forcing suffers from temporal drift once the inference rollout exceeds the training horizon; Frame Sink avoids temporal drift but yields lowdynamic, conservative motion. Ours (Disen-Forcing) is both drift-free and temporally dynamic. The bottom block isolates the contributions of our two components: context routing and Lreg.

Figure A11: Per-head temporal attention patterns in bidirectional Wan base models. Attention scores averaged over 50 prompts and diffusion timesteps for the pretrained bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B (left, 30 layers, 12 heads), Wan2.1-14B (middle, 40 layers, 40 heads), and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (right, 30 layers, 24 heads), before any causal AR training or distillation. All three models exhibit the same structural pattern observed in the AR-VDM variants of Fig. 2a: most heads attend predominantly to the current frame, while a sparse subset at specific layers shows concentrated attention to the initial frame.

Figure 4: Anchor-head positions are input invariant. (a) Each row plots a single prompt’s per-head initial-frame attention score. The same vertical stripes are coherent across all 50 rows, meaning the same subset of heads attends strongly to the initial frame regardless of prompt. (b) Each row plots the per-head cross-prompt mean attention score at one of the four diffusion timesteps. The four rows display the same vertical stripes, indicating timestep-invariance as well.

Figure A12: Reconstruction-based motion-proxy layer analysis. Left: reconstruction error for candidate layers 20, 26, 27, and 28 from warping the reference frame along cross-frame attention chains, normalized to a no-motion baseline (mean±std over motion prompts×seeds); layer 26 has the lowest error. Right: example attention-based point tracks on a running dog (top) and a leaping deer (bottom).

Table 1: Quantitative comparison on long video generation. Disen-Forcing is a distillation-time plug-in applied to Self-Forcing and Causal-Forcing. ∆Q Drift (↓) measures the imaging quality gap between the first and last segments. Best Total per horizon in bold.

Table 2: Ablation study on main components. We progressively add disentangled routing and motion-disentangling regularization to the Self-Forcing + Frame Sink baseline. We also ablate the anchor-head threshold τp, regularization weight λreg, regularization layer S, and anchor-head set A selection strategies. The component and threshold groups use four-layer regularization; other groups use layer 26 unless the regularization layer is varied. Rows are comparable within each group.

papers.title: Disen-Forcing: Disentangling Semantic Anchoring from Motion for Autoregressive Video Diffusion

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers have become the most powerful models for visual generation, but still suffer from massive computation costs. To solve this problem, feature caching has been proposed to cache the features of diffusion models in the previous computation steps and then reuse them in the following caching steps, which brings significant acceleration but also degradation in generation quality. To address this problem, this paper proposes Z-cache as a feature caching method that can maintain high-quality generation through self-reflection. Concretely, we observe that the error from feature caching tends to be sharply reduced after each full computation. Based on this observation, Z-Cache is designed to first predict the features in the future caching steps and then perform a full computation. After that, Z-Cache returns to the caching steps and re-predicts them based on the previous and the current computation steps, which brings correction in features. Experiments demonstrate that with Z-Cache, diffusion transformers achieve comparable generation quality to the original model but with faster inference speed, for instance, 6.22X acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation. Our code is released on GitHub.
bullets: Feature caching reduces diffusion-transformer computation but can degrade image quality.
Z-Cache predicts features for future caching steps, periodically performs full computation, and uses it to correct subsequent predictions.
Experiments report comparable generation quality with faster inference, including 6.22× acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation.
The method targets inference acceleration for diffusion-transformer-based visual generation.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Visualization of videos generated by Hunyuan Video with different feature caching methods. The annotated speedups denote FLOPs reductions relative to 50-step sampling.

Figure 3: Pipeline of Z-Cache. The figure uses the reverse-diffusion notation t, t − 1, . . . for visualization, while the text uses a sampling-order index that increases along denoising. Traditional feature caching forecasts an active window from a past full-computation anchor and directly moves to the next window. In contrast, Z-Cache treats the window as provisional: after obtaining the next scheduled full-computation anchor, it revisits the same window, constructs dual-anchor hidden estimates, re-samples the window trajectory, and commits the reflected window-end latent. Z-Cache therefore performs in-loop trajectory correction without adding extra full-computation steps.
Figure 4: The Trajectories of PCA components of hidden features. Z-Cache has the minimum divergence to the ground-truth comparing with other methods.

Figure 2: Visualization of the per-layer L1 error from feature caching. It is observed that there exists a periodic decline in L1 error, which is caused by the full-computation step in feature caching. The proposed Z-Cache utilizes this phenomenon and derives fewer cumulative errors.

Figure 5: Semantic stability under increasing cache interval N . As the cache interval increases, TaylorSeer gradually accumulates semantic drift, while Z-Cache maintains more stable object layout and visual identity.

Table 3: Quantitative comparison on text-to-video generation with HunyuanVideo on VBench. L-Speed and F-Speed are the latency and FLOPs speedups relative to the original 50-step model. Within each caching block, bold numbers indicate the best values, including ties.

Table 2: Full paired results for cache predictors on FLUX.1-dev with DrawBench. Rows are grouped by the equivalent cache interval N . Bold quality metrics indicate the better value within each Base/+Z-Cache pair; gray rows identify +Z-Cache. Parameters are abbreviated in parentheses: TeaCache uses (L), where L = rel_l1_thresh; SpeCa uses (B,D,m,M) = (base, decay, min, max); MagCache uses (T,K,R) = (th,K, retention).

Table 1: Quantitative comparison on class-to-image generation on ImageNet with DiT-XL/2. F-Speed denotes the FLOPs reduction relative to DDIM with 50 steps. Metrics marked with “-” are left unreported, as they were not provided in the original publications.
Table 6: Same-start local trajectories relative to the conditional local Full reference.
Table 5: Global latent trajectories relative to the shared Full reference.
Table 8: Two replay backends under the same TaylorSeer N = 6 schedule. Image quality uses DrawBench200; efficiency is a separate frozen-prompt A100 diagnostic.
Table 7: Fusion-function ablation. Bold marks the best point estimate in each SSIM, LPIPS, and IR column; no confidence intervals or human-preference study establish quality significance.

papers.tldr: Z-Cache accelerates diffusion transformers by predicting and self-correcting cached features while preserving generation quality.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have enabled generative video compression to reconstruct details lost during coding using pretrained spatiotemporal priors. However, a substantial gap remains between codec-induced degradation and the perturbation trajectories learned by flow-matching models. In this paper, we identify a compression-dependent directional mismatch that degradation-strength-based timestep calibration alone cannot resolve. Compressed latents remain strongly aligned across codec operating points, while their reconstruction residuals vary substantially in magnitude and direction. To bridge this gap, we propose RIFT, a Residual-Informed Flow Transfer framework for one-step generative video compression. At its core, RIFT introduces a Residual Geometry Inducer (RGI) that converts the pretrained flow prediction into a content-adaptive restoration update using decoder-visible codec cues. RGI integrates flow-timestep conditioning with a learned full-band residual-strength estimate and content-conditioned direction and gain modulation, aligning the orientation and magnitude of the update with the compression-dependent residual geometry. Extensive experiments on three public video compression benchmarks show that RIFT outperforms competing generative video compression methods. The code is publicly available on RIFT.
bullets: Compression artifacts differ in residual magnitude and direction, which timestep calibration alone cannot address.
RIFT uses decoder-visible codec cues to make restoration updates content-adaptive.
Its Residual Geometry Inducer combines flow-timestep conditioning with learned residual strength, direction, and gain modulation.
Experiments on three public video-compression benchmarks show RIFT outperforms competing generative compression methods.
The method targets one-step reconstruction using pretrained spatiotemporal priors.

papers.abstract: Video inpainting for object removal is scored over the whole hole, although the background behind the object is visible in other frames of the shot for some hole pixels and in no frame for others. A whole-hole score therefore mixes copying with generation and cannot show which of the two a remover does well. To separate the two, we propose recoverability-stratified evaluation, in which a point tracker run on the clean video labels each hole pixel by whether and how far away it is observed, so that fidelity and temporal stability can be reported per stratum against a copy reference. To reuse the observed content, we also propose evidence-guided sampling (EGS), which blends tracked colors into the clean-latent prediction of a video diffusion remover without training. On DAVIS, the perceptual advantage of three diffusion removers over flow propagation shrinks where the content is visible a few frames away (LPIPS difference-in-differences +0.046 to +0.056 against E2FGVI-HQ), and real paired captures show the same pattern for two of them. Their DAVIS hole warping error is two to four times that of ProPainter, and copying along clean-video tracks lowers their recoverable LPIPS by a quarter to two fifths. EGS closes 43% and 56% of the gap to this copy reference on held-out DAVIS when its colors come from clean-video tracks. With colors tracked on the masked input, a pre-registered confirmation finds no gain on MiniMax-Remover and a loss on ROSE. Diffusion removers thus leave observed content unused on DAVIS, and training-free reuse does not yet hold with tracked evidence.
bullets: Whole-hole metrics conflate pixels recoverable from other frames with pixels requiring generation.
A point-tracker-based evaluation stratifies fidelity and temporal stability by how recoverable each hole pixel is.
Evidence-guided sampling (EGS) injects tracked colors into diffusion predictions without additional training.
On DAVIS and paired real captures, diffusion advantages shrink for content visible nearby; their warping error is 2–4× ProPainter’s.
EGS closes 43% and 56% of the recoverable LPIPS gap with clean-video evidence, but masked-input evidence gives no gain for one remover and hurts another.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generators produce videos block by block from historical context. They are trained within a bounded horizon, whereas inference can extend far beyond it, causing temporal consistency to gradually decrease. Existing methods focus on eliminating this mismatch, but we instead ask whether the historical context used in training remains suitable for inference. Each block reads historical context in two stages, when denoising generates it and when committing writes it into the KV cache for later blocks. We find that older historical context such as the sink helps denoising but can hurt later blocks when read during committing, even in generators trained to read it there. We also show that as committing reads more preceding blocks, clip-to-clip Subject Consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines. We therefore propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. Each committing pass reads only the preceding block's stored KV, while denoising keeps the base historical context. Commit Forcing improves 60-second VBench Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 and 1.10 points. Its consistency gains extend to 240-second videos, and it achieves an 82.9% win rate in overall human preference on 120-second LongLive videos.
bullets: Long-video autoregressive generators lose temporal consistency when inference extends beyond their training horizon.
Older context can help denoising but harm later blocks during KV-cache committing, revealing a mismatch in how history is used.
Subject consistency rises, plateaus, and declines as committing reads more preceding blocks.
The training-free Commit Forcing rule makes committing read only the preceding block’s stored KV while preserving the base context for denoising.
It improves VBench Quality and Total across all six generators, with consistency gains extending to 240-second videos and an 82.9% human-preference win rate on 120-second videos.
